units.la: OVALE chirurgis carcinomatis genus est, cui dicitur, Noli me tangere: talis omnino mihi videtur in re sacramentaria existere quæstio de cœna Domini: quæ crebra sui inflammatione adeò solet intumescere, vt ne leuissimam quidem cōtrectationem admittat, quin bilem in nasum conciat. De hac igitur conuenienter cum poëta effari possumus, ---
units.tr: The surgeons have a kind of carcinoma called "Touch me not." The controversy over the Lord's Supper, a sacramental question, seems to me to be just like that. It so often swells with its own frequent inflammation that it will not tolerate even the lightest handling without stirring up bile in the nose. So I may fittingly speak here in the words of the poet: ---

units.la: laqueo tenet ambitiosi Consuetudo mali, tenet insanabile multos Scribendi cacoëthes, & ægro in corde senescit.
units.tr: "The custom of ambitious evil holds many in its snare; the incurable itch of writing holds them, and grows old in the sick heart."

units.la: Non tamen idcirco vsquequaq; spes omnis de curatione huius vlceris est abiicienda. fieri nanque potest, si expeditius malagma seu cataplasma imponatur, quod in se vim contineat emolliendi, aperiendi, pus educendi, & astringendi, ut vulnus ab omni sanie purgatum, citius coalescat. In aperiendo, Alexandri Macedonis imitemur industriā, qui fatalis in Gordieo plaustro iugi lora ---abdita opertis
units.tr: Still, hope of curing this ulcer should not be abandoned altogether. It can happen that if a quicker plaster or poultice is applied, one that has the power to soften, open, draw off pus, and also to constrict, the wound, cleansed of all its matter, will heal more quickly. In opening it, let us imitate the skill of Alexander the Macedonian, who, when at the Gordian wagon he could not loosen the fated thongs of the yoke hidden under their coverings, ---

units.la: Principiis, & utroq; caput celantia nodo, cùm soluere non posset, clauum, quo temoni iugum annectebatur, dissecuit, atq; sic protinus facillimè dissoluit. Similiter si nos clavum utriusque nodi, quo caput totius disputationis de coena Domini fixum latet, removerimus, & purulentum calumniarū & conuitiorum cruorem absterserimus, opis plurimum, rei alioqui deploratæ, conferemus. Ego itaque quasi ensis aut unguis in vomica, siquè forte dolorem, refricanda cicatrice malè obligata, recrudescere fecero, æquo id à me animo accipi ferríque debet: quando ad constantem sanationem tendit ac conducit. nulla enim ren e-dia, dia, vt summus ille orator inquit, quæ vulneribus adhibentur, tam faciunt dolorem, quàm quæ sunt salutaria.
units.tr: "...the beginnings, and the head hidden in a double knot," since he could not untie it, cut through the peg by which the yoke was fastened to the pole, and so at once loosened it very easily. Likewise, if we remove the peg of each knot, in which the head of the whole disputation about the Lord's Supper lies fixed and hidden, and wipe away the purulent blood of calumnies and abuse, we will bring great help to a matter otherwise despaired of. So, like a sword or a fingernail in an abscess, if I should perhaps stir up pain by reopening a badly bound scar, let it be received and borne by me with an even mind, since it aims at and leads to a lasting cure. For, as that great orator says, no remedies applied to wounds cause as much pain as those that are healing.

units.la: PAULUS Apostolus, abster-rens Timotheū à superuacaneis con-flictationibus & stultis ac ineruditis quæstionibus, quę disputationum pugnas nunquam finiendas pariunt magis quàm ędificationē[?] Dei quę est per-fidem: fabulis quæcunque sunt eius-modi annumerat, haud dubiè pro-pter summam vanitatem quæ talibus magna ex parte inesse solet. Dum enim homines inflati, mentéque cor-rupti, æmulatione & inuidia, ne aliis cedere videantur, extimulati, conten-tiones fouent, & ad maledicendū pe-tulantia ingeniorum prorumpunt & exultant: alij saniores, commoti tanta rerum indignitate, cum insanietibus insanire & ipsi quodammodo cogun-tur, vt stultis respondeant secundum stultitiam ipsorum, ne nimium sibi placeant sapiendo, néve alios parum providos secum in errorem abducat. Quo fit ut contentionis funiculus, quem quisque adse trahere conatur, protendatur longius antequàm rumpitur. Quippe verissimum est quod Galen° in Hippocratis calumniatore scripsit, οὐδὲν ὄξιν[?] ἀπεραντολογώτερον[?] αὐ-θέκτον. Quod tamè de arcu nimium tenso dici solet vulgò, idem ad extremum istiusmodi altercationibus & rixis, divino maximè urgente iudicio, eveniet, ut multis verbis ultro citróq; iactatis, dum montes parturiunt, mus tandem ridiculus exeat. In tragœdiis introducuntur Erinnyes, quarum instigatione res levibus quibusdam initiis in tantam perturbationem assurgunt, ut Poëtæ boni & actores industrij, cùm explicare argumeti exitum non possunt, ad Deum confugiant, & operam eius ad compescendos componendósque tumultus desiderent. Ostendunt itaque in mediis tumultibus, de sublimi numè aliquod ex machina, china, quod repente rebus in melius conuersis & compositis, finem fabulæ imponat.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul, when he warned Timothy away from vain disputes, and from foolish and unlearned questions, which produce quarrels of disputation that are never ended more than edification of God that is in faith, counted such things among fables, doubtless because of the great vanity that usually belongs to them for the most part. For when men, puffed up and corrupted in mind, are goaded by rivalry and envy, lest they seem to yield to others, they foster contentions, and the wantonness of their wits breaks out into slander and exults. Others, who are saner, moved by such great unworthiness of things, are in some measure forced to go mad with the madmen themselves, so as to answer fools according to their folly, lest they be too pleased with their own wisdom, or lead others, less cautious, with them into error. Hence it comes about that the cord of contention, which each one tries to draw toward himself, is stretched longer before it breaks. Indeed it is most true what Galen wrote against the calumniator of Hippocrates: nothing is more long-winded than a quarrel [ouden oxin aperantologoteron autheketon]. Yet what is commonly said of a bow drawn too tight applies in the end to altercations and brawls of this kind, especially when the divine judgment presses, so that after many words have been hurled back and forth, while the mountains labour, a ridiculous mouse at last comes forth. In tragedies the Furies are introduced, by whose instigation matters rise from slight beginnings into such great disturbance that good poets and skilled actors, when they cannot unfold the outcome of the plot, flee to God and call for his help to quell and settle the tumults. Thus they show, in the midst of the uproar, some deity from above on the machine, who suddenly, with affairs turned to the better and set in order, brings the play to an end.

units.la: Considera iam mihi tenuitatem suspicionum, quibus ceu scintillulis flamma dissensionis de cœna Domini (furiis infernalibus occulte suas tedas inferentibus) primùm exarsit: & mox linguastyloque contentiosorum quasi flabellis iurgiorum ventilata, in tam late grassans incendium, cui nemo iam, nisi Deus ὥσπερ ἀπὸ μηχανῆς θεὸς φανεὶς[?] restinguendo par esse queat, erupit.
units.tr: Now consider for me the slightness of the suspicions by which, like sparks, the flame of dissension over the Lord's Supper first broke out (the infernal Furies secretly bringing their torches), and then, fanned by the tongues and pens of the contentious as with fans of wrangling, burst into a fire spreading so widely that no one now can quench it except God, who appears as a god from the machine.

units.la: Anno protasin vides cū epitasi huius fabulæ? Cum igitur alii in primo atque altero actu reliqui nihil fecerint belli-co canendo, & iam diu hac de re in theatro Ecclesiæ plus quàm satis sit tumultuatum: tempus unà cum ratione postulat, prodire demum aliquē qui receptui canere incipiat, & subita commutatione facta, ferocientes compescat, resque turbatissimas componat. Sit ergo scriptum hoc qualecunque instar suspensæ tabulæ aut machinæ, cuius intuitu pudeat in posterum ἐπεξαγωγίζειν[?] eos qui de rebus verè ni-hili
units.tr: Do you see the protasis of this play together with the epitasis? Since others in the first and second acts have done nothing but sing of war, and for a long time now in the theatre of the Church there has been more than enough tumult about this matter, time and reason demand that someone at last come forward who will begin to sound the retreat, and, by a sudden change, restrain the fierce and settle the most troubled affairs. Let this writing, then, be whatever it is, like a hanging panel or machine, so that in future those who speak of things truly trifling should be ashamed to bring on the stage [epeisagōgizein]. ---

units.la: Quòd si forte hæc fabula suam nondū periodum assecuta fuerit, præludium saltem habeatur hoc, ad iustū finem & perfectā adusque determinationē.
units.tr: But if perhaps this play has not yet reached its period, let this at least be considered a prelude, for the just end and complete determination.

units.la: ¶ Dipnosophistica vox quàm sit conveniens præsenti tragœdiæ.
units.tr: The word Dipnosophistica, and how well it suits the present tragedy.

units.la: INCIDI nuper in libellum Δειπνολογικὸν[?], cuiº[?] auctor, cùm sibi propositisset quæstionē simplicem de cœna Domini, ad categorias, tanquam ad fontes rerum, deducendam, (egregio sanè conatu, si tā ingenuè ad veritatem pervestigandā, quàm assentatoriè ad auram popularem captandā, & ad invidiam aliis concitandam, suum institutum velut mantelum expassum flexisset) invehitur aliquoties acerbius & contumeliosius in Dipnosophistas: eos videlicet hac nota designans qui in negotio Eucharistico spirispiritualibus spiritualia comparantes iuxta doctrinam Apostolicam, spiritualiter diiudicari volunt, quæ animalis homo prudentiæ carnalis sensu nequit dignoscere. Apta quidé, meo quoque iudicio, dipnosophistarum appellatio est ad præsentem causam, sed in velites scurras qui istiusmodi cœnam, qualis in natura rerum nulla est, comminiscentes, tragicis clamoribus & execrationibus, panicum terrorem quendam animis hominum incutiunt, & oculos mentis perstringunt, ne cui fucus præstigiis verborum obductus, facile obuius appareat.
units.tr: I recently came upon a little book entitled Deipnologicon, whose author, having proposed a simple question about the Lord's Supper, set out to derive it from the categories, as from the sources of things. It was a fine effort, if he had bent his purpose as openly toward seeking out the truth as he bent it toward winning popular favour and stirring up hatred against others, like a cloak spread out to catch the wind. Several times he attacks the Dipnosophists more bitterly and abusively. He marks out by this label those who, in the matter of the Eucharist, compare spiritual things with spiritual things, following the Apostolic teaching, and want them judged spiritually, which the natural man with his carnal wisdom cannot discern. In my judgement the name Dipnosophists is indeed suitable for the present case. But these frivolous jesters, inventing a supper such as exists nowhere in nature, strike men's minds with a kind of panic by tragic cries and curses, and dazzle the eyes of the mind, so that no one, with his view clouded by the tricks of words, may easily see what lies before him.

units.la: Dolet igitur mihi (ut iure debebat omnibus) vehementer, quòd in hac ipsa causa, cùm alii nullum jam diu neque modum neque finem vociferandi, contra sensuum, rationis, naturæ, liberaliorisque doctrinæ iudiciū faciunt: alii immanem ac intolerandam barbariem, ignorantiæque caliginem in sacramētariam disputationem invehunt: contendentes Eucharistiæ quæstionem non perinde sicuti res alias, in suo quanque genere, à veteri, communi, perpetuáq; sacramentorum natura iudicari posse aut debere. id quod æque monstrosè statui dicique videtur, ac si quis aliquem professus hominem communibus omniū animatium proprietatibus exuat. Isti vero, sibi tantummodo sapientes, omittantur: nos, ne Deo pro suis donis ingrati simus, etsi dialecticen in pari dignitatis gradu cum Theologia non ponimꝰ, nedum ὥσπερ Δεῖγκον ἐπαινῶ ἢ αἰωτίεῳ[?], (quemadmodum Plato facit:) tamen libenter utimur illa, ut instrumento, ad exquirendā discernendámq; ab omni falso veritatem. Quò magis doleo cùm video etiā illos qui dialectices periti sunt, ideoque de vero & falso rectius iudicare poterant, in hoc negotio ita turpiter delirare, ac si eius artis elementa vix primoribus labris degustassent. Quis non miretur eum, qui Dipnosophistas erroris ex categoriis convincere instituit, distindistinctionem ab Aristotele categoriis præmissam,& tàtopere in omni disquisitione necessariam,( unde vel in primis utra pars de cœna Domini disceptantium sophisticè ageret, poterat cognosci) neglexisse, altóq; præteriisse silentio? Inde enim, quòd sunt aliqua quæ tam intra quàm extra orationis complexum, nomē unà cum re, aliqua sine re solum nomen cōmune habent, nullo negotio deprehenditur, cùm panis mysticus tum τῷ σύμ-πλοκῷ, tum αὐτὸ συμπλοκῆς, Christi corpus dicatur: nec tamen sub eandē corporis Christi definitionem cadat: quòd corporis Christi nomen pani neutrobi συνωνύμως, sed aut ὁμωνύ-μως, aut alia quapiam ratione tribuatur. Ergo valeat ea ratio quam Cyprianus & Augustinus è sacramentalibus sanctæ scripturæ locutionibus observatam, pro regula nobis reliquerunt: nempe, quòd in divinis mysteriis & sacramentis, res sensibiles & significantes, pro similitudine, non ipsa rerum veritate si[?]significatarum & sub intellectum cadentium rerum nomina recipiunt. Hæc pro veritate contra [illegible, ~6 letters] in causa Eucharistiæ placidis & moderatis ingeniis sufficere poterat. Quoniam vero contentiosi, vt pervicaces athletæ, prostrati nihilominus obstrepunt, & victi videri nolunt, nisi crura eis fracta fuerint: frangantur sanè & his crura, sic tamen vt viuant, & errore duplici liberetur.
units.tr: It therefore grieves me greatly (as it rightly should grieve everyone) that in this very cause, some have for a long time now shouted without any measure or end, against the judgement of the senses, of reason, of nature and of liberal learning; others have brought a huge and intolerable barbarism and the darkness of ignorance into the sacramentary debate, contending that the question of the Eucharist cannot or should not be judged as other things are, each in its own kind, by the ancient, common and perpetual nature of the sacraments. This seems as monstrous a claim as if someone professed to be a man and yet stripped him of the common properties of all living things. But those men, wise only in their own eyes, may be set aside. As for us, lest we be ungrateful to God for his gifts, although we do not put dialectic on the same level of dignity as theology (much less as Plato does, praising or blaming [ὥσπερ ... ἐπαινῶ ἢ αἰτιῶμαι]), we gladly use it as an instrument for seeking out truth and separating it from every falsehood. I grieve all the more when I see that even those who are skilled in dialectic, and therefore were able to judge more correctly between true and false, rave so shamefully in this business, as if they had barely tasted the first elements of that art. Who would not be amazed that the man who set out to convict the Dipnosophists of error from the categories has neglected, and passed over in silence, the distinction which Aristotle placed before the categories, and which is so necessary in every inquiry (by which one could at once recognise which side of the disputants was arguing sophistically)? For it is easily seen that some words have a common name together with the thing, both within the complex of a sentence and apart from it, while others have only a name without the thing. Thus the mystical bread is called the body of Christ, both in the complex sense [τῷ σύμπλοκῷ] and apart from the complex [αὐτὸ συμπλοκῆς], yet it does not fall under the same definition of the body of Christ. The name body of Christ is nowhere given to the bread synonymously [συνωνύμως], but either homonymously [ὁμωνύμως] or by some other way. Let that rule therefore stand, which Cyprian and Augustine, observing it from the sacramental expressions of holy Scripture, have left us as a standard: namely, that in the divine mysteries and sacraments, sensible and signifying things, by way of likeness, receive the names of the things signified and understood, not in the actual truth of the things. For the truth in this matter of the Eucharist, these things might have been enough for calm and moderate minds. But since the contentious, like stubborn athletes, though thrown down, still raise a clamour and refuse to admit defeat unless their legs are broken, then let their legs be broken, but in such a way that they live, and so they may be freed from a double error.

units.la: ¶ Errorum circa Eucharistiam bipartita origo, sermonis ignorantia, & superstitio, id est zelus citra scientiam.
units.tr: ¶ The twofold origin of errors about the Eucharist: ignorance of language, and superstition, that is, zeal without knowledge.

units.la: ARISTOTELES in sophisticis elenchis verissimam & vulgatissimã fallaciarum & captiosarum argumentationum causam adducit hāc, Ἐπει-δὴ ἔστιν αὐτὰ καθ' αὐτὰ τὰ σοφίσματα διαλέγεσθαι φησίς. ἀλλὰ τῆς ὀνόμασιν αὐτὴ τῆς σοφισμάτων [?] συμβόλοις, τὸ συμβαῖνον ἐπὶ τῆς ὀνομάτων, ἢ ἐπὶ τῆς σοφισμάτων μὴ συμβαίνειν.ι. Quoniam non licet nobis vna ferre nobiscum res de quibus per se ac solis disputemus: vtrimque pro rebus verbis, quasi quibusdam notis: quod in verusuvenit, idem in rebus existimamus usuvenire. Quando ait Philosophus, non bis ex eo quòd verba rerum notæ ha-bentur, videri quicquid verbis acci-dat, idem rebus ipsis contingere: summam probabilitatem ac verisimilitu-dinem eius insinuare voluit. quæ quidem in Eucharistiæ causa nonnullis tanta est, vt in hoc vnico fundamento insistere, eóque aut vincere aut cadere cogitent: alij perspicuitatem, alij feriam asseuerationè verborum Christi in Cœna: alij quòd non sit historica narratio, aut parabolica concio, vt multæ aliæ in scriptura sacra reperiũ-tur: sed in vltimo penè agone expres-sa oratio: & quid non præterea, obte-dunt. Semper tamen eòdem redit res, vt propterea quia verba notæ rerum sunt, idem in rebus, quod in verbis u-suvenit, usuvenire credatur. Cæterũ multos hac ratione decipi, Aristote-les pulchra comparatione ostendit, paulòpòst subiiciens, ὥσπερ οἱ μὴ δεινοὶ τὰς ψήφους φέρειν, [illegible, ~12 letters] ηεψυονΐα[?]· τὸν αὐτὸν ξόπον ἡ ὅπ[?] τῆς λόγων[?], οἱ τῆς ὀνομάτων τῆς δυνάμεως ἀπειρεῖ[?], παι-δευόμενοι[?] ἐκλογίζονται, ἢ αὐτοὶ διαλεγόμενοι, ἢ ἀλλήλων ἀκούοντες.ι. Vt ij qui rationes subducere nesciunt, à peritis falluntur: sic in disputatio-nibus, ij qui verborum vim ignorant, facile & cum ipsi disputant, & cum alios disputantes audiunt, falluntur atq; capiuntur. Est igitur ἡ τῆς τῆς ὀνομάτων δυνάμεως ἀπὸ[?]ειέα[?] certissima causa fallaciarum in quibuscunq; disputationibus. Diligenter notanda est ea ratio quam reddit Aristoteles, docens cur loco rerum, verbis, tanquam earum notis, in disputatione vtamur: quoniam videlicet res ipsas in disputationem afferre non possumus. Hoc cum in rebus diuinis & cæ-lestibus, nimis occultis & secretis, sit verissimum: recte scribit Augustinus, illas ita demonstrari nobis in scripturis, sicut potest capere sensus humanus: cum etiam rerum imaginibus in revelationibus tanquam verbis instruimur: atque idcirco, eiusdem authoris testimonio, diuinæ scripturæ à terreterreno & humano sensu, ad diuinū & cælestem nos erigentes, vsque ad ea verba descenderunt quibus inter se stultissimorum etiam vtitur cōsue-tudo. Et rursus, Multa diuina iisdem no-minibus appellātur quibus humana, cùm in-comparabili diuersitate seiuncta sint. Necta-men frustra eadem sunt rebus utrisque indita vocabula: nisi quia hæc cognita, quæ in quoti-diana consuetudine versantur, & experimē-tis usitatioribus[?] innotescunt, nonnullam ad illa sublimia præbent viā. Cùm igitur ma-gnum fit mysterium, humanæ rationi imperuestigabile, quomodo Christus foueat & enutriat Ecclesiam, quomodo item nos membra sumus corporis eiusdem, ex carne eius, & ex ossibus eius: hanc ob causam caro Christi pa-ne, sanguis eius vino in cœna Domi-ni adumbratur. Quòd si res illa sensi-bus pateret, neque verbis neque visi-bilibus elementis, ad excitādas men-tes in illius cōtemplationem & com-munionem, opus foret. nunc autem in tantùm nobis est abscōdita, ut hac manuductione verborum atq; signo-rum opus habeamus. Agnoscamus i-gitur συγκατάθεσιν[?] hanc diuinę sapientiæ & benignitatis in erudiendis no-bis, quam Chrysostomus & Augusti-nus non vno solùm in loco tantopere prædicant & commendant.
units.tr: Aristotle, in the Sophistical Refutations, gives this as the truest and most commonly recognised cause of fallacies and captious arguments: "Since we cannot discuss the things themselves in themselves, but use words as signs in place of things, we assume that what happens to the words also happens to the things" [ἐπεὶ δ' οὐκ ἔστιν αὐτὰ καθ' αὐτὰ τὰ πράγματα διαλέγεσθαι, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ὀνόμασιν ἀντὶ τῶν πραγμάτων συμβόλοις χρώμεθα, τὸ συμβαῖνον ἐπὶ τῶν ὀνομάτων ἐπὶ τῶν πραγμάτων ὑπολαμβάνομεν συμβαίνειν]. Since we cannot bring the things themselves into a dispute, we use words in their place, as certain marks, and what is true of the words we judge to be true of the things. When the Philosopher says that it is not because words are marks of things that whatever happens to the words is thought to happen to the things themselves, he meant to suggest a very great probability and likelihood. Indeed, in the case of the Eucharist, this is so strong for some that they think they must rest their whole case on this one foundation, and either conquer or fall by it: some rely on the clarity, others on the firm assertion of Christ's words at the Supper; others argue that it is not a historical narrative or a parabolic discourse, as many other passages of Scripture are, but an expression spoken almost at the last moment of a struggle; and they raise I know not what other objections. Yet the matter always comes back to this, that because words are marks of things, what is found in the words is believed to occur also in the things. Aristotle, however, shows with a fine comparison how many are deceived by this reasoning, adding shortly afterwards: "As those who are not skilled at reckoning the counters are deceived by experts, so in the same way those who do not know the power of words, whether they reason themselves or hear others reasoning, are deceived." [ὥσπερ οἱ μὴ δεινοὶ τὰς ψήφους φέρειν ... τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ... οἱ τῆς ὀνομάτων δυνάμεως ἄπειροι ... ἐκλογίζονται ... ἢ αὐτοὶ διαλεγόμενοι, ἢ ἀλλήλων ἀκούοντες]. As those who cannot work out the reckonings are deceived by the skilled, so in disputations those who do not know the force of words are easily deceived and caught, both when they dispute themselves and when they hear others disputing. Therefore ignorance of the power of words is the most certain cause of fallacies in every kind of dispute. The reason Aristotle gives, explaining why in argument we use words in place of things, as their signs, should be carefully noted: namely, that we cannot bring the things themselves into the discussion. This is most true of divine and heavenly things, which are too hidden and secret; and Augustine rightly writes that they are so presented to us in the Scriptures as the human mind can grasp them. Also, we are taught by images of things in revelations, as if by words; and for this reason, by the same author's testimony, the divine Scriptures, raising us from earthly and human sense up to the divine and heavenly, have descended even to those words which are used in common by the most foolish men. And again: Many divine things are called by the same names as human things, though they are separated by an incomparable difference. Yet those same names were not given to both kinds of thing in vain, but because these familiar things, which are in daily use and known through more common experience, offer some path to those sublime things. Since, then, it is a great mystery, unsearchable by human reason, how Christ cherishes and nourishes the Church, and how we too are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones, for this reason the flesh of Christ is foreshadowed by bread, and his blood by wine, in the Lord's Supper. If that thing lay open to the senses, there would be no need of words or visible elements to stir up minds to contemplate and share in it. But now it is so hidden from us that we need this guidance of words and signs. Let us therefore acknowledge this condescension of divine wisdom and goodness in teaching us, which Chrysostom and Augustine praise and commend so highly, not in one place only.

units.la: Videam{9} modò quidnā verbis Christi in coena mystica, de quibus lis est acciderit. Principiò ex eo quòd nomina diuersarū rerū, hoc est, panis visibilis & corporis Christi inuisibilis, itē vini & sanguinis, vno orationis ambi-tu, per copulam verbi substātiui, con-nectuntur, dicente Domino, de pane, Hoc est corpus meum: de vino, Hic est san-guis meus: nonne ex hac verborum connexione multi nimium fidenter rerum ipsarum coniunctionem quan-dam in coena statuunt? Ad hæc cùm visibilia elementa, quæ ante consecrationem panis & vinum dicuntur, a consecratione natiua & pristina nomina (sanctis præsertim patribus) de-ponūt: annon hinc multis persuasum etiametiamnū est, illa cum nominibus sub-stantiam quoque pristinam abiicere vel amittere? Tertiò constat hanc consuetudinem longo usu obtinuisse in Ecclesia, ut corporis & sanguinis Christi nomina pro pane & vino usurpari in oratione cōsueuerint: quo sen-su Cyprianus Christi corpus usque hodie creari & sanctificari, Chrysostomus illud etiam in actione cœnæ videri & palpari dixit. Quis hinc non credidit, substantias ascitorum nomi-num, corporis & sanguinis Christi, in locum abiectarum substantiarum pa-nis & vini succedere? Tres illæ opiniones, è nudis collectæ verbis, quoniam eodem fulcro niituntur, nec possunt pariter omnes veræ esse, (utramcun-que enim posueris, alteram perimes:) sequitur, ut fundamentum illarum est ruinosum, ita quod inde extruitur aut superstruitur, cōsistere non posse.
units.tr: Let me now see what the words of Christ in the mystical supper, which are the subject of this dispute, really mean. First, since the names of different things, namely the visible bread and the invisible body of Christ, and likewise the wine and the blood, are joined in one phrase through the copula of the substantive verb, the Lord saying of the bread This is my body, and of the wine This is my blood, do not many people too confidently infer from this connection of words some kind of conjunction of the things themselves in the supper? Again, since the visible elements, which before consecration are called bread and wine, after consecration lay aside their native and original names (especially in the view of the holy Fathers), has not this persuaded many, even to this day, that they also cast off or lose their former substance along with their names? Thirdly, it is established that this custom had prevailed in the Church by long usage, so that the names of the body and blood of Christ were commonly used in prayer for bread and wine. In this sense Cyprian said that the body of Christ is still created and sanctified today, and Chrysostom said that it is seen and handled in the action of the supper. Who, from this, has not believed that the substances of the borrowed names, the body and blood of Christ, take the place of the discarded substances of bread and wine? Those three opinions, gathered from bare words, rest on the same prop and cannot all be true together (for whichever one you posit, you destroy the others). It follows that, as the foundation of them is unsound, so whatever is built or raised upon it cannot stand.

units.la: Quandoquidem verò in cœnæ Dominicæ institutione, panis & vinū Χῷ συμπλοκῷ[?] corpus & sanguis Christi ab ipsomet Domino appellantur: delatum est hoc postea, quicquid est honoris & reuerentiæ, Christi verbo in Ecclesia, ut corpus & sanguis Do-mini etiam ἄνευ συμπλοκῆς [?] pro pane & vino Eucharistico, à consecratione maximè, ponerentur. Itaque formu-lis loquendi in primitiua Ecclesia re-ceptis, corpus Christi dicebatur iace-re in mensa, cadere de altari, manibus sacerdotis teneri, gestari, frangi, &c. vbi nimirum panis consecratus, licet nominatim non expressus, intellige-batur tamen: quia videlicet in prima sacra cœna corporis Christi nomẽ pa-ni esset attributum. Nihil ergo minus antiqui & orthodoxi patres sic hono-rificè de pane & vino consecrato lo-quentes, cogitarũt, quàm substantias panis & vini in vsu Eucharistiæ abii-cere, extrudere, negare: aut in substan-tias corporis & sanguinis Christi con-uertere, aut illa inter se colligare: ve-rum ut ostenderent quanto honori-ficentius de visibilibus elementis, postpostquam ad memoriam corporis & sanguinis Christi sanciendam & con-secrādam assumpta essent, sentirent, quàm aliâs communiter de istis senti-retur vulgò:ne(inquam)vilescerēt,aut in contemptum venirēt. Eam ob cau-sam, Christi verbis ad elementa acce-dentibus seu prolatis,non amplius natiuis suis appellationibus nominabā-tur:sed honoris & reverētiæ ergô no-vis nominibus corporis & sanguinis Christi ornabantur. Non igitur servi-li metu quodam ab initio, sed spiri-tuali potius libertate introductum est ac obtinuit: ut vocabula diversarum rerum inter se commutarentur: a-lioqui semper fuit,& adhuc est liberū in Ecclesia,panem ac vinum tam con-secratum quàm nondum consecra-tum, natiuis suis nominibus nuncu-pare. Cùm enim Apostolus non sit veritus panem & vinum, quamlibet consecratum , nihilominus pristinis suis appellationibus efferre: cui Chri-stiano post illum nō sit licitum idem facere? Augustinus certè ad infantes de visibilibus elementis consecratis, distinctè scribit, Quod vidistis, panis est & calix, quod vobis etiam oculi renuntiant: quod autem fides vestra postulat instrumen-da, panis est corpus Christi, & calix est san-guis. Porrò cùm in cœna Domini hoc vel in primis opus facto fit, vt nos ob-temperantes Christi mandato, tota mente ac cogitatione in verissimum ipsius corpus & sanguinem feramur, nullo iam amplius panis & vini habito quasi respectu: assuefacere voluerunt sancti patres ad hanc meditationem rerum cælestium suas & aliorum mentes, ne in terrenis & visibilibus elementis diutius hærerêt, sed his pro-pemodum neglectis, corda sursum levarent, ad agnum immaculatum in sacra mensa positum cõsiderandum.
units.tr: Since, however, in the institution of the Lord's Supper the bread and wine are called the body and blood of Christ by the Lord himself [συμπλοκῷ], it has since come about that whatever honour and reverence belongs to the word of Christ in the Church should also be applied, even without that connection [ἄνευ συμπλοκῆς], to the bread and wine of the Eucharist, chiefly after consecration. Thus, with the forms of speech received in the primitive Church, the body of Christ was said to lie on the table, to fall from the altar, to be held in the hands of the priest, to be carried about, to be broken, and so on, where clearly the consecrated bread was understood, although not named, because in the first sacred supper the name of the body of Christ had been given to the bread. Therefore the ancient and orthodox Fathers, speaking so reverently of the consecrated bread and wine, were thinking no more of casting out, expelling or denying the substances of bread and wine in the use of the Eucharist, or of converting them into the substances of the body and blood of Christ, or of blending them together, than they were of... rather, they meant to show how much more reverently the visible elements should be regarded, once they had been taken up to be sanctified and consecrated in memory of the body and blood of Christ, than they were commonly regarded otherwise: lest (I say) they should become cheapened or fall into contempt. For this reason, when the words of Christ were added to or spoken over the elements, they were no longer called by their native names, but out of honour and reverence were adorned with the new names of the body and blood of Christ. Therefore this practice was introduced and took hold not from any servile fear at the beginning, but rather from spiritual freedom: that the words of different things should be interchanged. Otherwise it has always been, and still is, free in the Church to call both bread and wine, whether consecrated or not yet consecrated, by their native names. For since the Apostle did not hesitate to call the bread and wine by their former names even though they were consecrated, why should it not be lawful for a Christian after him to do the same? Augustine certainly, writing to infants, distinguishes clearly about the consecrated visible elements: What you have seen is bread and cup, which your very eyes also report to you; but what your faith requires you to be instructed in is that the bread is the body of Christ, and the cup is the blood. Moreover, since in the Lord's Supper the chief task is that we, obeying the command of Christ, be carried with our whole mind and thought to his most true body and blood, with no regard now given to the bread and wine, the holy Fathers wished to accustom their own minds and those of others to this meditation on heavenly things, so that they should not cling longer to earthly and visible elements, but, these being almost disregarded, should lift up their hearts to contemplate the spotless Lamb placed on the holy table.

units.la: Progressu temporis, crescente in-scitia & superstitione, cùm iam religio esset panem consecratum nomi-ne suo natiuo appellare, coeptum est contra communem sensum, impudentiùs negari quòd panis consecratus substantiam suam pristinam retineat posteaquam & nomen proprium a- miserit,& alterum nomen à Domino ipso impositum induerit. Ad hoc con- firmandum citabantur testimonia pa- trum: quorum alij panis naturam transl- sumi, transelementari,& corpus Christi effici: alij ante consecrationem pa- nem,& vinum; post consecrationem corpus & sanguinem Christi vocari dixerunt. Trifariam itaque circa hunc locum,& quidem turpissimè, fuit er- ratum: primum in omissione pristina- rum appellationum panis & vini: dein- de in metalepsi adscitarum dictionum corporis & sanguinis Christi pro pa- ne & vino: tertiò in consecratione per- peram accepta. De prioribꝰ duobus multa iam diximus. Cùm autem rebꝰ tam portentosis, nihil vel in totarerum universitate, vel in sacris vel profanis literis patrocinetur aut suffragetur: Satan, vt est callidus, ne cui fraus sub- oleret, verba ipsa institutionis, extruedæ isti artolatriæ, pro basi subiecit. Quis enim sentiat, pestilentissimum verbi diuini hostem, Christi verba in hoc honoris fastigium euehere, vt his tanta vis & potentia conuertendi pa-nem in corpus ipsius tribuatur? Siquidem nemo pius dubitat quin Christus quod se velle dixerit, praestare possit. Cùm igitur panem & vinum corpꝰ & sanguinem suum esse disertè affirmet, nisi quis Dominum vel mendacij vel imbecillitatis velit arguere, concedat oportet, Christum in cœna & vera dicere & praestare quæ dicit posse. Hæc tam plausibilia quem non in errorem illiciant?
units.tr: As time went on, with ignorance and superstition growing, and when it had already become a matter of religion to call the consecrated bread by its native name, it began, against common sense, to be denied more shamelessly that the consecrated bread retains its former substance after it has lost its proper name and taken on another name imposed by the Lord himself. To confirm this, the testimonies of the Fathers were cited. Some of them said that the nature of the bread is transsubstantiated, transelementated, and made into the body of Christ; others said that before consecration it is called bread and wine, and after consecration the body and blood of Christ. Thus error arose about this passage in three ways, and most shamefully: first, in the omission of the former names of bread and wine; then in the metalepsis by which the words body and blood of Christ were adopted for bread and wine; and thirdly, in the perverse understanding of consecration. About the first two we have already said much. But since nothing, either in the whole universe of things or in sacred or profane letters, supports or lends its weight to such portentous claims, Satan, as he is crafty, so that no one should smell the fraud, placed the very words of institution as the foundation for building this idolatry of the bread. For who would think that the most pestilent enemy of the divine word would raise the words of Christ to such a height of honour that such great power and potency to convert the bread into his body should be attributed to them? For no pious person doubts that Christ can do what he said he wished to do. Since, therefore, he plainly affirms that the bread and wine are his body and blood, unless someone wishes to charge the Lord with lying or weakness, one must concede that Christ speaks truly in the supper and can do what he says. How could such plausible arguments not lead men into error?

units.la: Sciendum est autem, Satanam cum ministris suis pseudoprophetis & pseudapostolis, ad idololatriam stabiliendam, & seducedos miseros mortales, magnificè verbum Dei efferre & allegare: non quòd illi fides & obedientia verbo Dei adhibita, fit curæ: sed quò facilius in suos casses nos pertrahat[?], non prohibet, sed instigat, vt è verbis Christi malè intellectis & detortis idolum faciamus. Patitur ergo nos verbis Christi in cœna abuti ad artolatriam, & quoduis aliud erroris genus: nec illi dolet aut repugnat, quòd sic nobis ipsi placentes, verbum Dei facere magni & reuereri videmur. eo enim pacto, nõ ad Dei voluntatẽ, sed ad diaboli obsequiũ, nostrúmq; placitũ, diuina oracula dirigimus: & hic Satanæ lusus est, vt stulti, dum tricas illius ab vna parte euitare volunt, alte ra incidant. Quò minùs igitur terrerimus verborũ Christi abusus animadverteretur, consecrationis titulo fuit ornatus: qua non aliter quàm pharmaceutriæ & sagæ suis carminibus in excatationibus, sunt vsi. At verò Christus cœnam suam instituens, ad discipulos verba sua protulit, non ad immutandum aut confundendum naturas rerum: sed ad erudiendum illos, vt ex ore magistri discerent quid sibi ceremonia illa, tum temporis noua, & toti in posterum Ecclesiæ commendata, vellet: atque in hunc usum ad-huc hodie verba illa institutionis, quo-ties cœna Domini in Ecclesia cele-bratur, recitantur, ut accessuri ad mē-sam Dominicam, intelligant ad quid panem & vinum, ex Christi mandato & præscripto, sumant.
units.tr: It must be understood, however, that Satan, with his ministers, the false prophets and false apostles, magnificently extols and alleges the word of God in order to establish idolatry and to seduce wretched mortals. Not that he cares for faith and obedience paid to the word of God, but so that he may more easily draw us into his snares. He does not forbid but urges us to make an idol out of the words of Christ, badly understood and twisted. He therefore allows us to abuse the words of Christ in the supper for the worship of bread, and for any other kind of error; nor is he grieved or opposed by it, since, pleasing ourselves in this way, we seem to hold the word of God in high regard and reverence. For in this way we direct the divine oracles not to the will of God but to the service of the devil and to our own pleasure; and this is Satan's trick, that fools, while they wish to avoid his snares on one side, fall into another. Therefore, so that the abuse of Christ's words should be less noticed, it was adorned with the title of consecration, which they used just as sorceresses and witches use their charms in incantations. But Christ, instituting his supper, uttered his words to the disciples not to change or confuse the natures of things, but to teach them, so that from the mouth of the master they might learn what that ceremony, then new and to be commended to the whole Church for the future, meant. And to this end even today those words of institution are recited whenever the Lord's Supper is celebrated in the Church, so that those who are about to come to the Lord's table may understand for what purpose, by Christ's command and prescription, they take the bread and wine.

units.la: Iactantur magnifica de syllabis & apicibus viuentis Dei, quæ nobis cœ-lo ac terra firmiora esse debeant. Sanè si perpetuæ voluntati Dei, rerumque significatarum constantissimę verita-ti seruiant, non repugnent. An quæso rei in cœna à Christo sancitæ natura, minus apud nos, quàm nuda verborum auctoritas, valeat? Horumne syllabis & apicibus ad sacramenti incolumi-tatem & stabilitatem, an ad eius perniciem potius utamur? Mihi quidem certè maiori Deum iniuria afficere videtur is qui Christi verba in rei ab ipso institutæ euersionem detorquet, quàm qui, ut res saluas obtineat, verba Christi quomodocunque eò accommodat. Christũ suis in sacra cœnainstituenda[?] verbis, sacramentum fui corporis & sanguinis sancire uo-luisse, nemo, nisi qui os perfricuit, fa-cile negabit. At si visibilium elemen-torum, hoc est panis & vini, substan-tia tollatur è coena, (quod in trassub-stantiatione fieri necesse est) quomo-do analogia & similitudo, quàm signa ad res significatas habere debent, ut sint sacramenta, constabit? Quomo-do item corpus & sanguis Christi suâ tuebuntur substantiam, si realiter & substantialiter in vel sub pane insint, contineantur, aut delitescant? Nihi-lominus in talem sensum, naturae sa-crametorum usque adeò cõtrarium, verba Christi in coena sacra ab ad-uersariis rapiŭtur, qui interim de cer-titudine ac vi verborum Domini pro-lixè declamitare non cessant, ut suas saltem opiniones & delira venditèt.
units.tr: Magnificent claims are made about the syllables and letters of the living God, which ought to be firmer for us than heaven and earth. Certainly, if they serve the unchanging will of God and the most constant truth of the things signified, they do not conflict with our view. But I ask: in the Lord's Supper as instituted by Christ, does the nature of the thing carry less weight with us than the bare authority of the words? Do we use these syllables and letters to preserve and secure the sacrament, or rather to destroy it? To me, at least, he seems to wrong God far more who twists Christ's words into the overthrow of the thing Christ himself instituted, than he who, to keep the thing safe, somehow fits Christ's words to it. That Christ intended, in the words with which he instituted his supper, to ordain a sacrament of his body and blood, no one will easily deny except someone who has rubbed his face shameless. But if the substance of the visible elements, that is of bread and wine, is removed from the supper (which transubstantiation necessarily requires), how will it be established that there is the analogy and likeness which signs must have to the things signified, so that they are sacraments? Likewise, how will the body and blood of Christ keep their own substance, if they are really and substantially present in or under the bread, contained or hidden there? Nevertheless, the words of Christ in the holy supper are dragged by our opponents into such a sense, so contrary to the nature of the sacraments, while they meanwhile never cease to declaim at length about the certainty and power of the Lord's words, so that at least they may peddle their own opinions and their absurdities.

units.la: ¶ Quinam paralogismi frequetius in quæstionem de coena Domini incidant.
units.tr: ¶ What paralogisms most often arise in the question about the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Sir[?] bene penitus singula excutia-mus, quæ sibi proponūt exquireda qui certandi vincendique studio disputant: nullum eorum in contentione de coena Domini praetermissum esse deprehendemus, ut sunt, χ⊙ [?], ψευδ⊙ [?], ἀπρόσδοξον [?], σολοικισμὸς [?], ἢ ἀδολεσχία.
units.tr: Indeed, if we examine thoroughly each of the things that those who dispute with a zeal for contending and winning set before themselves to be sought out, we shall find that none of them has been omitted in the contention over the Lord's Supper, namely [χ⊙?], falsehood [ψευδ⊙?], unexpectedness [ἀπρόσδοξον?], solecism [σολοικισμὸς?], or babbling [ἀδολεσχία].

units.la: Primùm enim multa afferuntur in medium, quae contrarium concludere videntur, nec tamen concludunt. Nonnulla sunt manifestè falsa, contra opinionem, & communem sensum. Accedit etiam barbaries & nugandi ad fastidium usque consuetudo. Nos pauca quaedam obiter perstringemus.
units.tr: For first, many arguments are brought forward which seem to conclude the contrary but in fact do not conclude. Some are manifestly false, contrary to opinion and common sense. Added to these are barbarism and a habit of trifling to the point of tedium. We shall touch briefly on a few of them.

units.la: Captionum aliae sunt in verbis, aliae in rebus. In verbis, usitatissima est homonymia, quae multiplici significatione unius verbi, falsam conclusionem facit. Ita vox sacramenti definitur à multis invisibilis gratiae visibilis forma vel signum. In quo sensu dicit Augustinus, impios & infideles sacramentum premere dentibus, rem vero sacramenti non percipere. Qui iam sacramenti nomine non solùm signum, sed & rem significatam accipiunt, si inde colligant, rem significatam ore sumi, vel ab impiis percipi, homonymia vocabuli ludùt. Sic quoque corpus & sanguis Christi proprie dicitur de eo quod pro nobis in crucem oblatum, & qui pro nobis effusus est in remissionem peccatorum. Hoc corpus & hic sanguis ore non sumitur, nec ab infidelibus, ut Augustinus multis in locis docet: cùm verò corpus & sanguis Christi pro pane & vino usurpantur, tunc & ore capiuntur & ab infidelibus.
units.tr: Some fallacies lie in words, others in things. In words, the most common is equivocation, which by the manifold meaning of a single word produces a false conclusion. Thus the word "sacrament" is defined by many as a visible form or sign of invisible grace. In this sense Augustine says that the impious and unbelievers press the sacrament with their teeth, but do not receive the reality of the sacrament. Those who now take "sacrament" to mean not only the sign but also the thing signified, and infer from this that the thing signified is taken by the mouth or received by the impious, are misled by the ambiguity of the word. So too "the body and blood of Christ" is properly said of that which was offered for us on the cross, and which was poured out for us for the remission of sins. This body and this blood are not taken by the mouth, nor by unbelievers, as Augustine teaches in many places. But when the body and blood of Christ are used for bread and wine, then they are taken by the mouth and by unbelievers.

units.la: Inter fallacias extra dictionem è rebus ipsis natas, illa maximè in quæstionem de cœna Domini cadit quę à dicto secundum quid argumentatur, ac infert dictú simpliciter. Nam de hoc cõtrouertitur hodie inter partes, An panis & vinum dicantur corpus & sanguis Christi proprie & simpliciter, an secundum quid. Vbi non obseruant aduersarij, quod Aristoteli est τῷ λέγεσθαι, id Augustino dici se-cundum quendam modum, & quo-dammodo: qua formula cùm Augu-stinus aliquoties vtatur in definienda verborū Christi vera & genuina sen-tentia, vt fateatur secundum quendā modum panem dici corpus Christi: mirum est, aduersarios adhuc audere affirmare, simpliciter panem Christi corpus esse, cùm τῇ & ἁπλῶς ἢ νοερῶς ita sint opposita, vt stante altero sit necesse alterum tolli.
units.tr: Among the fallacies arising from the things themselves, not from the words, that one falls most often into the question about the Lord's Supper which argues from what is said in a certain respect and infers what is said absolutely. For today the parties dispute whether bread and wine are called the body and blood of Christ properly and simply, or only in a certain respect. Here our opponents do not observe that what Aristotle calls "to be said" (τῷ λέγεσθαι), Augustine calls being said in a certain manner and in some way. Since Augustine uses this formula several times when he defines the true and genuine sense of Christ's words, so as to confess that bread is called the body of Christ in a certain manner, it is strange that our opponents still dare to affirm that bread is simply the body of Christ, when "in a certain respect" (τῇ) and "simply or intellectually" (ἁπλῶς ἢ νοερῶς) are so opposed that, one being affirmed, the other must necessarily be removed.

units.la: Porrò, si panis & vinum Eucharisti-æ à cõsecratione non sunt amplius ἀχεῖς, sed τὰ τῆ ἐσ τι: nec propter se cõ-municantur, sed participantur pro-pter aliud rerum genus, corpus videlicet & sanguinem Christi: (quemadmodum Bernardus de annulo inue-stituræ loquitur, Annulus non valet quicquam: hæreditas est, quam quærebam.) qua igitur fronte vt panis & vinū sic quoque corpus & sanguis Christi pro fun-damento venditantur: cùm ex pane & vino orta, in corpore & sanguine Christi desinat relatio? Relatiuorum certè natura hoc fert & postulat, vt non absolutè aut simpliciter, sed cōparatè, hoc est mutua cōsideratione, spectentur & explicentur. Quando itaque propriis, quibus explicentur, nominibus destituuntur relatiua, cogit necessitas & vocabulorum inopia, vt explicationem vel à fundamento, vel à termino mutuemur. Vnde fit vt panis & vinum, postquam ad vsum cœnæ sacræ assumpta sunt, ab iis quibuscum conuertuntur, & à suo termino, denominentur, vt intelligatur ad quid fieri debeat panis & vini in cœna Domini relatio. Qua igitur ratione alibi caro Christi verè dicitur esse cibus, & sanguis verè dicitur esse potus: eodem planè pacto vice versa in cœna sacra, panis dicitur esse Christi corpus, & vinum sanguis, propter mutuum respectum quę illa ex Christi sermone ac institutione inter se habet. Hinc colligi potest, quàm insul-sè ac intricatè res diuersarum categoriarum in disputatione de cœna Domini confundantur, cùm realiter & substantialiter iuncta putantur & dicuntur, quæ nō nisi relatiuorum more, tanquam signa cum rebus suis significatis, coniunguntur. Qua de re mox plura, Deo volente, dicemus.
units.tr: Furthermore, if the bread and wine of the Eucharist, after consecration, are no longer mere (ἀχεῖς) things but things that are relative (τὰ τῆ ἐσ τι), and are not shared for their own sake but are partaken of for the sake of another kind of thing, namely the body and blood of Christ (as Bernard speaks of the ring of investiture: "The ring is worth nothing; it is the inheritance that I was seeking"), then with what face is the body and blood of Christ peddled as the foundation, just as bread and wine are, when the relation that arises from bread and wine ceases in the body and blood of Christ? The very nature of relatives certainly bears and requires that they be regarded and explained not absolutely or simply, but comparatively, that is, by mutual consideration. When, therefore, relatives lack the proper names by which they might be explained, the necessity and poverty of words compels us to borrow the explanation either from the foundation or from the term. Hence it comes about that bread and wine, after they have been taken up for the use of the holy supper, are named from those with which they are correlated and from their term, so that it may be understood what relation bread and wine ought to have in the Lord's Supper. Therefore, just as in another place the flesh of Christ is truly said to be food and his blood truly said to be drink, so in the holy supper, in exactly the opposite way, bread is said to be the body of Christ and wine the blood, on account of the mutual respect which these things have to one another by Christ's word and institution. From this it can be gathered how foolishly and confusedly things of different categories are mixed together in the dispute about the Lord's Supper, when things that are joined only in the manner of relatives, as signs with the things they signify, are thought and said to be really and substantially joined. On this matter we shall say more shortly, God willing.

units.la: Alter paralogismus rerum in negotio cœnæ frequentissimus, est, Τοῦ ἐ-λέγχ[?] ἄγνοια. Huc pertinent longæ declamationes de omnipotentia Dei, de coniunctione duarum naturarum in Christo, de sessione ad dexteram Dei: quæ omnia planè sunt ἀπερ[?]σδιό-νυστα[?], quantùm ad propositam quæstionem attinet: multò etiam magis, encomia illa de maiestate, veritate & constantia verbi Dei: item, quæ de imbecillitate peruersitatéque humanæ sapientiæ, rationis, sensuum, in rebus diuinis, ad pauorem panicum iniiciẽdum, haud aliter aggregantur & exaggeratur, quàm Mithridaticum bellum & Cannẽsis pugna adscisceban-tur ab aduocato in leuissima causa, ut est apud Martialem. Quid enim quæ-so ad rem præsentem facit, quòd in Christo diuinitas cum humanitate est hypostaticè vnita? Quasi verò pro-pterea verba Christi in cœna sacra sint ἁπλῶς[?] & κυρίως, non οὐχ ὡς πρὸς τι[?], ἢ ἐν μέρει accipienda. Quasi idcirco su-matur Christi corpus & sanguis Christi, ore, & ab infidelibus, quia sedet ad dexteram Dei, & data ei est omnis potestas in cœlo & terra: aut quasi mox Dei verbum negetur, mendacitér[?] arguatur, quia transsubstantiatio aut consubstantiatio non conceditur.
units.tr: Another paralogism of things, very frequent in the business of the supper, is ignorance of the point in question (τοῦ ἐλέγχ[ου] ἄγνοια). To this belong the long declamations about the omnipotence of God, the union of the two natures in Christ, the session at the right hand of God: all of which are plainly beside the point (ἀπερισδιόνυστα) as far as the question proposed is concerned. Much more so are those encomiums on the majesty, truth and constancy of the word of God; likewise those things said about the weakness and perversity of human wisdom, reason and senses in divine matters, which are heaped up and magnified to strike a panic terror, no differently than the Mithridatic war and the battle of Cannae are dragged in by an advocate in the most trivial case, as in Martial. For what, I ask, does it have to do with the present matter that in Christ divinity is hypostatically united with humanity? As if for that reason the words of Christ in the holy supper were to be taken simply and properly, and not "not as in relation to something" (οὐχ ὡς πρὸς τι) or "in part" (ἐν μέρει). As if the body and blood of Christ were taken by the mouth, and by unbelievers, because he sits at the right hand of God and all power in heaven and earth has been given to him; or as if the word of God were straightway denied and charged with falsehood, because transubstantiation or consubstantiation is not conceded.

units.la: Quid verò vsitatius est aduer-sariis, in probatione suæ opinionis, quàm τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ λαμβάνειν, quā principij petitionem vocant, quando idem probationis loco adducūt de quo agitur? Sic enim argumentantur: Cor-pus & sanguis Christi ore corporeo sumuntur, quia panis & vinum sunt corpus & sanguis Christi, quæ ore sumuntur.
units.tr: And what is more usual for our opponents, in proving their opinion, than to beg the question (τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ λαμβάνειν), which they call petitio principii, when they bring forward as proof the very point under dispute? For they argue thus: "The body and blood of Christ are taken by the bodily mouth, because the bread and wine, which are taken by the mouth, are the body and blood of Christ."

units.la: Ex vitiosis consequētibus sic con-cludunt: Fides nec quærit nec disputat de veritate & potentia verbi diuini, sed assen-titur simpliciter: quare absque omni dubita-tione credendum est, panem esse corpus Christi. Ratio humana in plerisque fallitur, quae ad res diuinas pertinent: ergo non est vel ra-tioni vel sensibus fidendum in re sacramen-taria. Deus qui potest omnia, efficere potest ut panis sit corpus Christi: ergo panis est Chri-sti corpus. Qui spiritum in coena Domini vr-gent, diffident inter se, varie interpretando: ergo errant. Maxima pars hominum probat literalem sensum in coena: ergo genuinus est & verus. Allegoriis deceptus est Cle-mens Alexandrinus, Origenes, & multi alij: ergo & hodie decipiuntur qui allegorice ver-ba Christi in coena interpretantur. Spiritua-lis verborum Christi sententia magnas turbas excitat in Ecclesia: ergo est impia & falsa. Huc bona pars conuitiorum & scō-matum, quae ab aduersariis in doctri-nam sacramentariam coniiciuntur, referri potest.
units.tr: From faulty consequences they conclude thus: "Faith neither seeks nor disputes about the truth and power of the divine word, but simply assents; therefore without any doubt it must be believed that the bread is the body of Christ. Human reason is deceived in most things that pertain to divine matters; therefore neither reason nor the senses are to be trusted in the sacramental matter. God, who can do all things, can bring it about that the bread is the body of Christ; therefore the bread is the body of Christ. Those who press the spiritual sense in the Lord's Supper disagree among themselves, interpreting variously; therefore they are in error. The greater part of men approves the literal sense in the supper; therefore it is genuine and true. Clement of Alexandria, Origen and many others were deceived by allegories; therefore those who today interpret the words of Christ in the supper allegorically are also deceived. The spiritual sense of Christ's words stirs up great disturbances in the Church; therefore it is impious and false." To this may be referred the greater part of the insults and taunts which our opponents hurl at the sacramentarian doctrine.

units.la: Tribuitur etiam sententiae quod proprium est personarum eam profitentium: Qui sic sentiunt, viri boni sunt: ergo ergo sententia eorum est bona. Impiè viuunt: ergo & malè sentiunt qui spiritualem sensum in cœna Domini tuentur. Hæc & similia multa, quæ splendidis amplificationibus & exornationibus (vt phaleræ ad populum) ostentantur, dum altius mecum reputo & perpendo, demiror attonitus, quomodo nugæ plusquàm aniles tā persuaderi dementer, quàm temerè creditæ in opinione hominū etiam doctissimorum vsque adeò pertinaciter atque diu hærere potuerint. Continere igitur me non valeo, quin illud Ethnici Poëtæ in ἀδολεσχίαν & ἀ-περαντολογίαν vitilitigatorum exclamē,
units.tr: The opinion also takes on what is characteristic of those who profess it: "Those who think this way are good men; therefore their opinion is good. They live impiously; therefore those who defend a spiritual sense in the Lord's Supper also think wrongly." These and many similar arguments, displayed with showy amplifications and embellishments (like trappings for the crowd), leave me astonished when I reflect and weigh them more deeply. How could such absurdities, more than old-womanish, be so foolishly believed, and how could things rashly accepted have stuck so stubbornly and so long in the opinion of men, even the most learned? I cannot restrain myself from crying out with that line of the pagan poet about the babbling and endless wrangling of quibblers: [2]

units.la: ----quantum est in rebus inane!
units.tr: "...how much emptiness there is in things!"

units.la: Video enim huic controuersiæ haud secus accidisse ac cæteris rebus magnis, famæ aliqua ex parte obnoxiis, solet contingere, quas multa plerunque vana & inania, vt phalangem in acie leuis armatura, comitantur. Vbi mihi in mentē [?] venit eiꝰ dicti quod Plutarchus grauis autor alicubi scribit, ὡς πολέμως [?], ἢ ἀπεχάσεως [?] πολλὰ τὰ ναυά [?]
units.tr: For I see that this controversy has fared no differently from other great matters, which are somewhat exposed to notoriety and which usually attract many vain and empty things, as a light-armed troop accompanies the phalanx in battle. Here there comes to mind that saying which the grave author Plutarch somewhere writes: [ὡς πολέμως, ἢ ἀπεχάσεως πολλὰ τὰ ναυά]

units.la: C. i.
units.tr: C. i.

units.la: In bellis quidem certè saepe, quod falsò creditum est, temporis diuturnitate veri vicem obtinuit. Quantam consternationem totis nonnunquam exercitibus panici pauores, nulla ferè aut momentanea occasiuncula oborti, imprimūr, qui praecipites in fugam, nemine etiam persequente, interdum ruunt? Nos si de dissidio Eucharistico verum fateri volumus, dicemus illud ab initio hucusque meris rumusculis & terroribus panicis cōstitisse, atque etiamnum constare. Ampullae enim sesquipedalium verborum in defensionem τοῦ ῥητοῦ profusae: item extenuationes ac detestationes contrariae sententiae, quid quaeso aliud sunt quàm λῆρος ἢ φλυαρία, & plane γλαυκοκατο-ωλεινά[?], si ad rem propositam aequa lance omnia pensentur & exigantur? Equidem credo Deum permisisse hoc Satanae furoribus nostro tempore, in praesenti causa maximè, ut in lucis angelum transformatus, personam induceret in organis suis ministri veritatis, tis, pietatis & iustitiæ: quò exercita-tiores aduersus illius insidias atque technas redderentur electorum sen-sus,ne mox,simulac præclarū aliquod è sacrosancta scriptura prolatum elo-gium audierint, assentiantur, quasi is qui tale quippiam iactat, omnino ve-rum asserat, nec ipse errare, nec alios seducere queat. Nam si cacodæmon, qua est impudentia, non est veritus, dominum, magistrum, & caput no-strum, verbis è scriptura depromptis aggredi: quid mirum, si membra corporis Christi simili ratione aggredia-tur,vt tentando circumueniat? Christus sanè præsentiens has diabolicas fraudes, repudiauit prorsus testimo-nium, quamlibet verum, sibi à Sata-na datum. Paulus item ægrè ferens spiritum Pythonis è puella diuinatri-ce, clamantem quòd Apostoli serui Dei excelsissimi essent, viam salutis annuntiantes,compescuit: non vt sal-si argueret, aut in suspicionem addu-ceret salutis annunciationem ore A-[?] postolorum factam, quam spiritus im mundus approbarat: sed potius, ut e-rudiretur Ecclesia Christi cunctis te-poribus, non mox pro verbo Dei arri-piendum esse quod ut verbum Dei sonaret, sed probandos esse[?] spiritus an ex Deo sint. Cum enim Deus, qui solus probe novit quid in homine sit, infallibili oraculo pronuntiet, om-ne figmentum cogitationum huma-ni cordis ab adolescentia sua adeo-que omni tempore malum esse dun-taxat: debebat hoc merito omnem in nobis confidentiam iudicandique li-centiam & temeritatem cohibere: ne facile nostris aliorumve placitis in-dulgentes, nimium addicti essemus, aut tribueremus: quin certo scientes nihil esse magis in procliui, homini praesertim mortali, quam fallere & decipi: aequo patieremur animo nos ab aliis admoneri, & nostra corrigi. Nunc autē quoniam caecus est amor sui, suum etiam cuique maxime est pulchrum & sanctum. Praeterea cor homihominis suos habet anfractus, recef-sus, gyros & latebras, quibus se instar serpentis involuit & contorquet: ut scite divinus uates, postquam cor vafrũ suõ omnia dixisset, quęsierit, Ecquis cognoscat illud? idémque mox voce Dei ἢ [?]θεολογικῶς sumpta, significanter sibi-ipse per subiectionem respõderit, Ego Dominus & cor perscrutor & renes explo-ro. Quod mihi quidẽ haud citra singu-lare quandã emphasin à Propheta sic enuntiatũ videtur: cuiusmodi nimirũ & illud est quod Paulus Apostol° scri-bes ad Corinthios, ex 94 Psalmo cita-tũ, sæculari sapiétiæ opponit, ad hunc modũ, Novit Dominus cogitationes sapiê-tium, quòd sunt vanæ. Ubi tametsi uel im primis dănatur τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς ἡ ψυχικὴ αἰσθήσεως[?], cui stultitia & aduer-sa sunt quæcunque ad Legẽ & spiritũ Dei pertinẽt: pravitas tamẽ in miseris mortalibus latens, adhuc tanta est, ut sæpe etiam divinis in sermonibus & negotiis, in quibus (inquam) si usquã alias, & tutò consistere, & firmissimè colligere nobis videmur, ratiocina-tiones nostrae euanescant. Extremam hanc humanarum opinionum inani-tatem sapientis. regis concionator in quaestionibus de finibus bonorum & malorum luculeter notauit. Nos ve-rò, si probè singulas religionis nostrae partes, quae hodie in contentionem veniunt, exploremus: parem, si non maiorem in plerisque, hominum futilitatem inueniemus: cuius rei gustū aliquem, nisi fallor, facto in quęstione de coena Domini periculo, hactenus praebuimus. Consequēs est, ut ulce-ri jam aperto & à sanie purgato, em-plastrum imponamus, quo firmius a-stringatur & coalescat.
units.tr: In wars, indeed, it often happens that what was falsely believed has, through the lapse of time, taken the place of truth. How great a consternation do panic fears sometimes cause in whole armies, arising from almost no occasion or from a momentary trifle, so that men at times rush headlong into flight with no one even pursuing them? If we wish to speak the truth about the Eucharistic dispute, we will say that it has consisted from the beginning until now of mere rumours and panic terrors, and still does. For the bombastic words poured out in defence of the literal text [τοῦ ῥητοῦ], likewise the belittlings and denunciations of the opposing view: what, I ask, are they other than nonsense [λῆρος] and foolish talk [φλυαρία], and plainly downright owl-eyed twaddle [γλαυκοκατοωλεινά], if everything is weighed and measured on an even scale against the matter at hand? I indeed believe that God has permitted this, in our time especially in the present cause, to the fury of Satan, so that he, transformed into an angel of light, might put on a persona in the instruments of the ministers of truth, of piety and of justice. The senses of the elect would thus be trained more keenly against his snares and tricks, lest, as soon as they hear some notable saying brought forth from holy Scripture, they assent at once, as if the one who utters such a thing could assert only what is true and could neither err himself nor lead others astray. For if the demon, in his impudence, did not shrink from assailing our Lord, Master and Head with words taken from Scripture, what wonder if he attacks the members of Christ's body in a similar way, to circumvent them by temptation? Christ, indeed, foreseeing these diabolical frauds, utterly rejected a testimony given to him by Satan, however true it was. Paul likewise, troubled by the spirit of Python in the fortune-telling girl, who cried out that the apostles were servants of the Most High God announcing the way of salvation, silenced it. He did not do so to accuse the apostles or to cast suspicion on the proclamation of salvation made by their mouths, which the unclean spirit had approved; rather, he did so that the Church of Christ in all ages might learn not to seize at once upon whatever sounds like the word of God as the word of God, but that spirits must be tested to see whether they are from God. For since God, who alone knows well what is in man, pronounces by infallible oracle that every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart is evil from its youth, and therefore evil at all times, this ought rightly to restrain in us all confidence, all licence and rashness in judging. Lest, readily indulging our own or others' opinions, we become too attached to them or ascribe too much to them, we should, knowing for certain that nothing is more prone to happen, especially to a mortal man, than to deceive and be deceived, bear calmly to be admonished by others and to have our own views corrected. But now, since self-love is blind, each person's own view seems to him especially beautiful and holy. Besides, the human heart has its windings, recesses, turns and hiding-places, in which it coils and twists itself like a serpent. So the divine seer, after saying that the heart is deceitful above all things, asked, "Who can know it?", and then, taking up the voice of God and speaking theologically, significantly answered himself by way of apposition: "I the Lord search the heart and try the reins." This seems to me to have been pronounced by the prophet with a certain singular emphasis. Of the same kind is what the Apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians and citing Psalm 94, sets against worldly wisdom: "The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain." Here, although the mind of the flesh [τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός], that is the psychic perception [ἡ ψυχικὴ αἴσθησις], to which folly is opposed and to which all things pertaining to the Law and Spirit of God are adverse, is chiefly condemned, the perversity still lying hidden in wretched mortals is so great that often even our reasonings vanish in divine discourses and affairs, in which, I say, if anywhere, we seem to stand securely and to gather our conclusions most firmly. The preacher of the wise king noted this utmost emptiness of human opinions most clearly in his inquiries into the chief good and evil. But if we properly examine the individual parts of our religion that today come into dispute, we will find, if not greater, then at least equal futility of men in most of them. Of this we have, unless I am mistaken, given some taste so far, in the trial made in the question about the Lord's Supper. It follows that, the ulcer now being opened and cleansed of its matter, we should apply a plaster by which it may be more firmly bound and may grow together.

units.la: ¶ Quidnam cœna Domini cum verbo Dei & reliquis sacramentis habeat com-mune;[?] & quid proprium:
units.tr: What the Lord's Supper has in common with the Word of God and the other sacraments, and what is peculiar to it:

units.la: Vt Eucharistiae quaestionem & causam à communi perpetuaque sacramentorum natura iudicari nolunt, has causas allegant:tum, quòd sacramenta prorsus arbitraria & fortuita sint, tum quòd à se inuicem in infini-tum varient atque distent.
units.tr: As they will not have the question and cause of the Eucharist judged from the common and perpetual nature of the sacraments, they allege these reasons: first, that sacraments are altogether arbitrary and accidental; and second, that they vary and differ from one another to infinity.

units.la: Posita verò sacramentorum inter se in infinitum distantia, cùm infini-tarũ rerum nulla disciplinabilis queat esse comprehensio, fieri non potest vt de sacramentis quicquam certi tra-datur aut percipiatur. Idem de fortuitis & contingētibus est iudicium, è quibus nihil firmiter concluditur.
units.tr: But if the differences between the sacraments are infinite, then, since no infinite things can be comprehended by any teaching, nothing certain can be handed down or grasped about the sacraments. The same judgment holds for things accidental and contingent, from which nothing can be firmly concluded.

units.la: Deo autem, qui rectissimo consilio, ordine, numero, pondere & mensura cōdidit & administrat vniuersa, quo-modo potuit quippiā institui fortu-itum, præsertim ad solennem ipsius cultum? Sunto sanè sacramenta Deo autori suo arbitraria, vt pro illius sapientia & voluntate, quotiescunque lubitum est, mutentur: quemadmodum legimus in Testamento veteri, pro temporis atque populi ratione, plura diuersaque Legis fuisse sacramenta, quæ postea sub Testamento nouo desierunt, referēte Augustino, in pauciora numero, actu faciliora,
units.tr: But God, who with most sound counsel created and governs all things in order, number, weight and measure, how could anything accidental be instituted by him, especially for his solemn worship? Let sacraments certainly be arbitrary with respect to God their author, so that they may be changed whenever it pleases him, according to his wisdom and will. As we read in the Old Testament, according to the time and the people, there were many and diverse sacraments of the Law, which afterwards ceased under the New Testament, as Augustine reports: they became fewer in number, easier in practice, more august in understanding, and finally purer in observance.

units.la: c. iiii. intellectu augustiora, obseruatu de-niq; castiora. Num vero idcirco ho-rum ratio minus constans aut perpe-tua existimari debet?Fatemur quidē, quatenꝰ testatur Apostolus scientiā abolitum iri, vbi quod perfectum est venerit, & nos nunc ex parte cognos-cere, & per speculū cernere in ænig-mate. At in Ecclesia adhuc militante, durante Verbi & sacramentorū œco-nomia, non dubitamus affirmare, sa-cramenta omnia & Eucharistiam in-primis, ad eundem quem cum verbo communem præfixū scopum habet, tedere, ad Christum (inquā) qui Le-gis finis est, ad salutem omnī credēti.
units.tr: c. iiii. Does it follow, then, that their reason ought to be thought less constant or less lasting? We grant indeed, as the Apostle testifies, that knowledge will be done away when what is perfect has come, and that we now know in part and see through a mirror in a riddle. But in the Church still militant, while the economy of the Word and the sacraments endures, we do not hesitate to affirm that all sacraments, and the Eucharist above all, aim at the same goal which they share in common with the Word, namely Christ (I say), who is the end of the Law, unto salvation for everyone who believes.

units.la: Cùm sacramenta Augustino dicuntur visibilia quædam verba, in-nuit vir sanctus, Deum, quò certiores nos reddat suæ voluntatis, non ver-bis tātum, sed & rebus ipsis ante ocu-los positis nos instituere & docere. Duobus quippe præstantissimis sen-sibus hominis obiicit quæ ad animū nostrum deportari vult, quò firmius &tenacius hæreant. Et quoniā verba sunt πτερόεντα[?], hoc est alata, quæ quasi volant irreuocabilia,& nisi literis mandentur, ad posteros & absentes perferri nequeunt: Christus consulturus nostræ ruditati memoriam fui corporis & sanguinis,quò durabilior foret,in visibilibus signis, pani & vino quodammodo alligare voluit. Adde quòd vehementius mouent quę in oculos quàm quæ in aures incurrunt. Quantum C. Cęsaris interfecti vestimenta cruenta à M. Antonio in cōcione prolata, potuerint ad populum Romanum in tyrannicidas concitandum, historiæ testantur. Quantum pondus vaticiniis Ieremiæ attulit baltheus ille lumbaris ad Euphratem in foramine petræ abscōditus? Item fidelia à figulo coëmpta, & in oculis virorum confracta? Item lora & iuga collo Prophetæ accommodata? Quibus verba Prophetæ, res illas visibiles explicantia, postquā fuerunt adiecta, populus Iudaicus inde multò certius sua fata, sibi à Deo im-pendētia;agnoscere potuit. Ita in sa-cra cœna,vbi ad res visibiles memo-randarum rerū nomina accesserunt, nihil iam ad perfectissimam commemo-rationē requiri videtur amplius. Dum enim visus noster cernit panē & vinum ,& aures audiunt nomina corporis & sanguinis Christi: sugge-ritur fideli menti,tum, ad quid nobis in cœna Domini panis & vinum co-ducant: tum, quid corpus & sanguis Christi nobis ad vitam, maximè æter-nam,conferant. Siquidè ista mutuā quasi operam sibi inuicem declaran-dis præstant, ut corporis & sanguinis Christi vocabula indicent quò panis & vinum referantur & respiciant: ac vicissim panis & vinum ostendant, corpus Christi pro nobis traditum, esurientibus iustitiam, esse panem il-lum vitæ de cœlo,qui dat vitam mun-do: sanguinem Christi pro nobis in remissionem peccatorum effusum, esse potum illum cælestem, quem sitiensitientes iustitiam si biberint, nunquam sitiant sed sustententur ad vitam æternam. Esset itaq; panis & vinum in coena Domini [illegible, ~4 letters] quasi πρόσωπα[?], nisi gererent nomina corporis & sanguinis Christi diuinitus imposita. Simulac vero novis insignibus à Christo pani & vino inditis, perceptu fuerit quorsum tendant: tunc revera nobis sunt visibilia verba & sacramenta. Hoc enim ipso, quòd dicuntur corpus & sanguis Christi, loquuntur nobis quodammodo, quidnam in hac coena, fides nostra instruenda, potissimum attendere debeat. Unde enim citius quæso memoria corporis & sanguinis Christi excitetur in animis nostris, nisi eorundem expressis nominibus? Quem vero non plus moveat panis visibilis in medium allatus, & nomine corporis Christi pro nobis tradit i insignit⁹, quàm si nudis verbis dicatur, panis de cœlo Christi caro est, exposita pro mundi vita? Si quis fidem daturus alicui, dicat se illi manum præbere, nemo est vulgaris con- suetudinis atque sermonis adeò igna- rus ac rudis, quin promissum sibi istis verbis fieri intelligat. vbi autem præ- ter verba sic facta, manus etiam ipsa porrigitur, idem quod antea confir- matur atque promittitur, & nihil a- liud. Dubium tamen non est, quin manus re ipsa data, verbis aliàs nudis pondus afferat & vehementius mo- ueat. Interim quis ita insulsus est, vt si is qui manum præbet, serió & san- cte affirmet se fidem suam alteri da- re, alius quispiam statim cogitet aut colligat, fidem porrigentis manum, realiter & substantialiter vel è manu cõuersam, vel cum, in, sub manu con- iunctam esse, quia videlicet bonus vir dixerit fidem, non manum, à se datâ, licet etiam manus data sit? Ad hunc modum pollicetur Christus se datu- rum panē de cœlo, qui sit caro ipsius pro vita mundi exponenda: quā vti- que postea in cruce pro nobis in mor- tē, sicuti promiserat, tradidit. Huius sacrifisacrificij semel peracti memoriam, non minus familiariter, quàm solen-niter consecraturus, in omnē posteri-tatem delegit è fructibus terræ, panē & vinum, quibus tanquam sigillis propterea nomina sui corporis & sanguinis impressit & insculpsit, quò certius ac evidentius beneficij nobis in cruce exhibiti admoniti, Deo sempi-ternas gratias agamus, inque fide & charitate in dies magis magisq; pro-ficiamus. Propius ergo & efficacius panis & vinum corporis & sanguinis Christi nominibus ornata, mentibus nostris infigunt & consignant ean-dem veritatem, quam prius ex verbo Dei percepimus. Audientes enim, corpus Christi pro nobis esse traditū, & sanguinem fusum in remissionem peccatorum, si vel modica fide imbu-ti simus, mirum in modum nos affici necesse est. Ad hæc, si coràm intuëamur symbola sacra ab ipsomet Domi-no memoriæ sui corporis & sanguinis dedicata, tantò magis afficimur quātò evidentius panis terrenus & visi-bilis panem cœlestem ac invisibilem, potus terrenus & visibilis potum invisibilem & cœlestem & nomine & imagine refert.
units.tr: When Augustine calls sacraments visible words, the holy man hints that God, in order to make us more certain of his will, teaches and instructs us not only by words but also by things set before our eyes. For he presents to two most excellent senses of man what he wishes to be carried into our mind, so that it may cling more firmly and tenaciously. And since words are winged [πτερόεντα], that is, alate, and as it were fly away irrevocably, and cannot be conveyed to posterity and to the absent unless they are committed to writing, Christ, intending to provide for our dullness, wished in some way to bind the memory of his body and blood to visible signs, bread and wine, so that it might be more lasting. Add that things which enter the eyes move us more vehemently than things which enter the ears. Histories attest how greatly the bloody garments of the murdered Gaius Caesar, displayed by Mark Antony in a sermon, could stir the Roman people against the tyrannicides. How much weight did that linen girdle, hidden in a cleft of the rock by the Euphrates, lend to the prophecies of Jeremiah? Likewise the earthen vessels bought from the potter and broken before the men's eyes? Likewise the thongs and yokes fitted to the prophet's neck? Once the prophet's words explaining those visible things were added, the Jewish people could recognise far more certainly their fate impending from God. So in the holy Supper, where the names of the memorable things have been added to visible things, nothing further seems needed for the most perfect remembrance. For while our sight beholds bread and wine, and our ears hear the names of the body and blood of Christ, it is suggested to the faithful mind both why bread and wine are brought to us in the Lord's Supper, and what the body and blood of Christ confer on us for life, above all for eternal life.
