For these things render mutual service to each other in making clear: the words "body and blood of Christ" indicate to what the bread and wine refer and relate; and conversely, the bread and wine show that the body of Christ was given for us, that it is the bread of life from heaven for the hungry for righteousness, which gives life to the world; that the blood of Christ was shed for us for the remission of sins, that it is the heavenly drink which, if the thirsting for righteousness drink it, they will never thirst but be sustained unto eternal life. Thus the bread and wine in the Lord's Supper would be [illegible] as it were masks [πρόσωπα], unless they bore the names of the body and blood of Christ divinely imposed. But as soon as, by the new marks given by Christ to the bread and wine, it has been perceived to what they tend, then truly they become for us visible words and sacraments. For by this very fact that they are called the body and blood of Christ, they speak to us, in a way, of what our faith ought chiefly to attend to in this Supper. For, I ask, from what else could the memory of the body and blood of Christ be more quickly roused in our minds, unless by their express names? Who would not be moved more by the visible bread brought forward and marked with the name of the body of Christ given for us, than if it were said in bare words, "the bread from heaven is the flesh of Christ, given up for the life of the world"? If someone who is going to give a pledge to another says that he holds out his hand to him, there is no one so ignorant and rude in ordinary custom and speech as not to understand that the promise is being made to him in those words. But when, besides the words so spoken, the hand itself is also extended, the same thing that was previously affirmed and promised is confirmed, and nothing else. Yet there is no doubt that the hand actually given adds weight to words otherwise bare and moves more vehemently. Meanwhile, who is so foolish that, if the man who offers his hand solemnly and sincerely affirms that he is giving his pledge to another, someone else immediately thinks or concludes that the pledge of the one extending his hand is really and substantially either converted out of the hand, or joined with, in, or under the hand, simply because the good man said "pledge", not "hand", although a hand was also given? In this manner Christ promises that he will give the bread from heaven, which is his flesh to be offered up for the life of the world; which flesh he afterwards indeed delivered up for us on the cross to death, as he had promised. Intending to consecrate the memory of this sacrifice, once accomplished, no less familiarly than solemnly, for all posterity, he chose from the fruits of the earth bread and wine, into which, as into seals, he stamped and engraved the names of his body and blood, so that we, more certainly and evidently reminded of the benefit exhibited to us on the cross, may give eternal thanks to God and make ever greater progress in faith and charity day by day. Therefore bread and wine, adorned with the names of the body and blood of Christ, more closely and effectively fix in our minds and seal the same truth which we previously received from the Word of God. For on hearing that the body of Christ was given for us, and his blood shed for the remission of sins, if we are imbued with even a little faith, we must be affected in a wonderful way. Moreover, if we look on with our own eyes at the sacred symbols which the Lord himself dedicated to the memory of his body and blood, we are affected all the more, as the earthly and visible bread represents both in name and image the heavenly and invisible bread, and the earthly and visible drink the invisible and heavenly drink.

units.la: Hoc nimirū illud ipsum est quod apud Augustinū toties recurrit, Solet res quæ significat, eius rei quā significat, nomine nuncupari. At nequis cogitet, regulam modò positam ad locutiones sacramentales Eucharistiæ præcipuè non pertinere: perpēdat paulò altius quæ idem ille pater de hac consuetu-dine scripturæ sacræ, tam specialiter quàm generaliter, in epistola ad Bo-nifacium admonet, sic scribens: Si sacramenta similitudinem quandam earum rerum quarū sacramenta sunt, non haberent, omnino sacramenta non essent. Ex hacaut similitudine plerunque rerum ipsarum nominā sortiuntur. Sicut ergo secundum quendam modum, sacramentum corporis Christi, corpus Christi est, & sacrametum sanguinis Christi, sanguis Christi est ; ita sacramētum fidei fides est. &c. Porrò significatio quæ ob si-militumilitudinem signi cum re significata, signo est imposita, Christo autore, nihil est aliud quã fundamēti ad suū terminum applicatio: quæ cùm magis proprie enunciari non possit, signum, hoc est fundamentum, nomen rei significatæ, tanquam sui termini, sortitur. Qui vnione sacramentalem malūt causam dicere ob quam panis Christi corpus vocetur: hi rectè quidē sentirēt, si eiusmodi coniunctionem ponerent qualis solet esse relatiuorū inter sese, & rerum ipsarum cum suis notis, siue verbis, siue visibilibus signis. Vt igitur vnaquæque vox, siue scriptilis, siue enuntiata, suam rem significatam, sibi adiunctam & inclusam continet: ita quoque sacramēta, vtpote verba visibilia, significãdo ea quæ diuina impositione & similitudine seu imagine quadam adumbrant, vnum quodammodo cum illis fiunt. Videntur autem isti realem & sub-stantialem magis quàm sacramen-talem vnionem ponere, quotquot realiter & substantialiter panē Chri-sti corpus esse cōtendūt. Quare cùm loquantur pugnantia, non modò contra naturam & rationem, verū etiam adversus semetipsos, sinamus eos a-bundare suo sensu.
units.tr: This is certainly that very principle which recurs so often in Augustine: "A thing that signifies is usually named by the name of the thing it signifies." But lest anyone think that the rule just laid down does not pertain especially to the sacramental expressions of the Eucharist, let him weigh a little more deeply what that same Father, both specifically and generally, admonishes in his letter to Boniface about this custom of Holy Scripture, writing thus: "If sacraments did not have a certain likeness to those things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. From this likeness they generally take the names of the things themselves. So, therefore, in a certain manner the sacrament of the body of Christ is the body of Christ, and the sacrament of the blood of Christ is the blood of Christ; so the sacrament of faith is faith, etc." Moreover, the signification which, on account of the likeness, has been imposed on the sign together with the thing signified, by the authority of Christ, is nothing other than the application of a foundation to its end; and since it cannot be expressed more properly, the sign, that is the foundation, receives the name of the thing signified, as of its own term. Those who prefer to call the sacramental union the cause on account of which the bread is called the body of Christ would rightly judge if they posited such a conjunction as is wont to exist between correlatives, and between things themselves and their marks, whether words or visible signs. Just as every word, whether written or spoken, contains its signified thing joined and enclosed with it, so too sacraments, as visible words, by signifying those things which by divine appointment they shadow forth by likeness or some image, in some way become one with them. Yet those who maintain that the bread of Christ is really and substantially the body of Christ seem to posit a real and substantial union rather than a sacramental one. Therefore, since they speak contradictions, not only against nature and reason but also against themselves, let us allow them to abound in their own sense.

units.la: ¶ Quid sit ὀρθοτομεῖν[?] τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀ-ληθείας in negotio Eucharistiæ.
units.tr: What it is to rightly divide the word of truth [ὀρθοτομεῖν τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας] in the matter of the Eucharist.

units.la: QVOD Paulus unicè commen-dans Timotheo requirit in v-noquoque Ecclesię doctore, ut rectè secet sermonē veritatis: dici nō potest quàm sit pręteritum à multis in hac causa. Quidam panem & vinum an-te ἁγιασμὸν[?] dicit antitypa nominari Theodoreto & Macario,( quibus ta-mē magnam facit iniuriam ) post cō-secrationem negat τύπος esse. Quòd si ante consecrationem antitypa dici merentur, frustra accedit verbum ad elementum, ut existat sacramentum: quia hoc sine verbo accedente jam ante habet. Si post consecrationem typi non amplius sunt, quomodo hāc appellationem deponere aut amitte-re re potuerunt, quin unà substantiam, qua typi nituntur, amiserint?
units.tr: That Paul commends to Timothy above all else, requiring it of every teacher in the Church, that he rightly divide the word of truth, is something that is passed over by many in this matter, more than can be said. Some call the bread and wine antitypes before the sanctification [ἁγιασμόν], as Theodoret and Macarius are named (though they do them great wrong), but after consecration they deny that they are types [τύπος]. But if they deserve to be called antitypes before consecration, the word comes to the element in vain so that it may become a sacrament, since it already has this without the word coming to it. If after consecration they are no longer types, how could they put off or lose this appellation without also losing the substance on which the types rest?

units.la: Idem ille panē & corpus Christi, vinum & sanguinem Christi pariter, in fundamento & fundamenti loco ponit: cùm nō modò rerum ipsarum, sed etiam vocabulorum diuersa col-locatio in Christi sermone, contrariū doceat & euincat. Quis verò unquā rerum dialecticarum mediocriter peritus illi concesserit, quòd terminus cum fundamento pro uno eodémque habeatur? perinde enim hoc est, ac si principium & finis unum ac idem esse dicerentur. A fundamento enim oritur, in termino definit relatio. Cū igitur panis & vinum sint τὰ πρός τι [?], & ad corpus & sanguinem Christi refe-rantur: conuerti quidem illa inter se posunt, vt Ioannis 6 caro Christi verè dicitur esse cibus & panis, san-guis Christi verè dicitur esse potus: in coena verò vice versa, panis dicitur esse Christi corpus, vinum dicitur es-se Christi sanguis: confundi autem & unius fundamenti loco poni illa nunquam possunt.
units.tr: The same man places bread and the body of Christ, wine and the blood of Christ, alike as foundation and in the place of foundation, when not only the things themselves but also the different arrangement of the words in Christ's speech teaches and proves the opposite. Who indeed, moderately skilled in dialectic, would concede to him that terminus and foundation are held to be one and the same? For it is just as if principle and end were said to be one and the same: relation arises from a foundation and is defined in its terminus. Since therefore bread and wine are relatives [τὰ πρός τι] and are referred to the body and blood of Christ, they can indeed be converted into one another, as in John 6 the flesh of Christ is truly called food and bread, and his blood is truly called drink; but in the Supper, conversely, bread is called the body of Christ and wine is called the blood of Christ. Yet they can never be confused and put in the place of one foundation.

units.la: Idem scribit, Christum dixisse ad discipulos simul accumbentes, Hoc quod ore sumitis, seu comeditis & bibitis, est meum corpus, & meus sanguis: cum præceptum de edendo antecedat hæc verba, Hoc est corpus meũ, ideoque haud dubiè panē terrenum & visibilem spectet, quem nimirum acceptum, eis tradidit comedédum: sicuti mox vinum, seu vini poculum, propinauitdelibandum. Quid igitur, inquies, an non simul corpus & sanguinem domini edebant & bibebāt? omnino, sed nō labiis, ore, atquelin-gua, ut S. patres scribere dicis tu quidem,at nō probas. Ego verò de pane & vino aperte confiteor, licet ore capiantur, edantur & bibantur, hoc tamen non fieri ad pascendum ventrē, sed mentem: id quod expresse testantur verba mox subsequētia, Facite hoc in mei memoriam. Quid quæso voluit Dominus fieri in sui memoriam? An non edi panem,& bibi vinum?Quod si negare voles, Paulus te redarguet, sic scribens, Quotiescunque comederitis panem hunc,& hoc poculum biberitis,mortem Domini annunciate. Cui omnino respondet quod dixit Dominus, Facite hoc in mei memoriam.
units.tr: The same writer says that Christ spoke to the disciples as they reclined together: "What you take in the mouth, that is, eat and drink, is my body and my blood." But the command about eating precedes the words This is my body, and so without doubt it looks to earthly and visible bread, which he took and handed to them to be eaten, just as presently he offered the wine, or cup of wine, to be tasted. "What then," you will say, "did they not eat and drink the body and blood of the Lord together?" Certainly, but not with the lips, mouth and tongue, as you indeed say the holy Fathers write, but you do not prove it. I for my part plainly confess concerning bread and wine that, although they are taken, eaten and drunk by the mouth, this is not done to feed the belly but the mind. The words that follow immediately express this: Do this in remembrance of me. What, I ask, did the Lord want done in his remembrance? Was not bread eaten and wine drunk? But if you wish to deny this, Paul will refute you, writing thus: "As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord." To this, what the Lord said, Do this in remembrance of me, fully answers.

units.la: Alius quispiam sic discerpit & lacerat verius quam secat institutionis verba, ut, Hoc est corpus meum, in signo & substantia sacramenti ponat, quod pro vobis traditur. Item, Facite hoc in meâ commemorationem, pro fine & re signi-ficata. Quanto rectius istis omnibus Irenaeus & Augustinus dicunt, Eucha-ristiam duplici rerum genere consta-re, quarum alterum sit terrenum, visi-bilia scilicet elementa, alterum coe-leste, invisibilis (inquâ) gratia corpo-ris & sanguinis Christi? Qua propor-tione, verba institutionis coenae Do-minicae rectissimè sic distribuuntur, ut prius mandatum Christi de edēdo & bibendo, res terrenas & visibiles concernat, panē dico & vinum, quae, postquam accepit, gratias egit, & dedit discipulis, subiecit, Edite, panè intelligens: & paulò post, Bibite, de vino loquens. Reliqua omnia quæ his ad-iuncta sunt verba, ad mysterij expli-cationem pertinent. primùm enim, quidnam visibilia elementa, panis & vinum, fidelibus esse debeat indicat istis verbis, Hoc est corpus meum, Hic est sanguis meus. Deinde, quid actiones e-dendi & bibendi conducat, admonet, dicendo, Facite hoc in mei memoriā. Quid ergo est commemorandum in actione coenæ mysticæ? hoc nempe, Christi corpus pro nobis traditum, esse nobis panem illum de cœlo, qui dat vitam mundo, &c. sanguinem Christi pro nobis effusum in remissionem peccatorum, esse potum illum cœlestem, qui sitientes iustitiam ita reficiat ut sitire desinant. Terrenis igitur ac vi-sibilibus signis & actionibus ex altera parte cœlestia respondent: pani & vi-no, corpus & sanguis Christi: manducationi & potationi externæ, commemoratio interior quæ spiritualē man-ducationem & communicationem corporis & sanguinis Christi cōpre-hendit.Ergo ista verba Domini, Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur, ni-hil aliud, nisi quo panis referriânobis[?] debet, explanant. Hoc facite in mei memoriam, actiones edēdi & bibendi ex-plicat. Illud membrum, Quod pro vobis traditur, Qui pro vobis effunditur, osten-dit quid in Christi corpore & sangui-nerecolere & commemorare debea-mus. Nec est vero consentaneum quod illi dictitat qui hoc membrum ab antecedentibus auellunt, ut finē[?] sacramenti in eo collocent. Hic e-nim non est Eucharistiæ & sacramen-ti, sed potius passionis mortisq; Do-minicæ finis, quæ pro nobis & in re-missionem peccatorum nostrorum à Christo est persoluta. Nobis vero ad perfruēdum per verbum & sacramē-ta cōmunicatur: cuius perfruitionis, cœna Domini manifestā præ se fert, non allusionem modo, verum etiam consignationem & contestationem, quòd Deus præparavit ab æterno hanc mensam nobis, in qua agnus ille immaculatus, ab initio mundi immolatus, & in ara crucis demum tostus, proponitur comedendus, & sanguis eius bibendus, quo nimirum animi nostri esurientes sitientesq; iustitiam refocillentur ac satientur. Hæc igi-tur meditantes interim dum ad mē-sam Domini adstamus, veneratione debita panè & vinum, haud amplius vulgari in pretio, ut res profanas, ha-bemus, sed ut sancto usui destinata mandato Domini usurpamus, & vir-tute huius cibi ac potus, quàm diu in deserto huius mundi & in via sumus, nosmet corroboramus, donec vene-rimus ad montem Domini, ubi vide-bimus eum non amplius per speculũ in ænigmate, ut nunc, sed facie ad fa-ciem sicuti est. Ubi hunc portum sa-lutis nostræ attigerimus, nihil erit quod insuper desideremus.
units.tr: Another person tears and mangles the words of institution more than he cuts them, so that he places "This is my body" in the sign and substance of the sacrament, "which is given for you" likewise, and "Do this in my commemoration" in the end and the thing signified. How much more correctly Irenaeus and Augustine say, against all these, that the Eucharist consists of a double kind of things: one earthly, namely the visible elements, and the other heavenly, namely (I mean) the invisible grace of the body and blood of Christ. In this proportion the words of the institution of the Lord's Supper are most rightly distributed. The first command of Christ, about eating and drinking, concerns the earthly and visible things, I mean bread and wine: when he had taken them, given thanks and given them to the disciples, he added "Eat", meaning bread, and a little later "Drink", speaking of wine. All the remaining words added to these pertain to the explanation of the mystery. For first, he indicates in these words, "This is my body", "This is my blood", what the visible elements, bread and wine, ought to be for the faithful. Then he admonishes what the actions of eating and drinking serve, saying, "Do this in remembrance of me." What then is to be commemorated in the action of the mystical supper? Namely this: that the body of Christ given for us is to us that bread from heaven which gives life to the world, and so on; that the blood of Christ poured out for us for the remission of sins is that heavenly drink which so refreshes those who thirst for righteousness that they cease to thirst. Thus to the earthly and visible signs and actions the heavenly things correspond on the other side: to bread and wine, the body and blood of Christ; to external eating and drinking, the inward commemoration which comprehends the spiritual eating and the communication of the body and blood of Christ. Therefore those words of the Lord, "This is my body, which is given for you", explain nothing other than to what the bread must be referred for us. "Do this in my remembrance" explains the actions of eating and drinking. That clause, "which is given for you", "which is poured out for you", shows what we ought to revere and commemorate in the body and blood of Christ. Nor is it truly consistent with what those assert who tear this clause away from what precedes it, in order to place the end of the sacrament there. For here is not the end of the Eucharist and the sacrament, but rather of the passion and death of the Lord, which Christ paid for us and for the remission of our sins. But it is communicated to us to enjoy through the word and the sacraments. The Lord's Supper manifestly displays of this enjoyment not only an allusion but also a sealing and attestation: that God from eternity prepared this table for us, on which that spotless lamb, slain from the beginning of the world and at last roasted on the altar of the cross, is set forth to be eaten, and his blood to be drunk, so that our hungry and thirsty souls may be refreshed and satisfied with righteousness. Meditating on these things meanwhile, as we stand at the Lord's table, we hold bread and wine with due reverence, no longer at the common price as profane things, but we use them as destined for holy use by the Lord's command. By the power of this food and drink we strengthen ourselves, as long as we are in the wilderness of this world and on the way, until we come to the mountain of the Lord, where we shall see him no longer through a mirror in a riddle, as now, but face to face as he is. When we have reached this harbour of our salvation, there will be nothing further that we desire.

units.la: DIALECTICA COENÆ DOMINICAE EXPLI-catio.
units.tr: DIALECTICA COENÆ DOMINICAE EXPLICATIO.

units.la: Duo illa rerum in cœna Domini-ni propositarū genera bifariam considerantur: Absolutè & Comparatè. Absolutè considerata, tam visibilia elementa, panis & vinum, quàm inuisibilis gratia, hoc est corpus & sanguis Christi, ad substantiarum categoriam pertinent: atque sic nomina sua natiua, prout illis primùm sunt imposita, retinent, & ut propria sibi vendicant.Panis igitur & vinum, corpus item & sanguis Christi, si propriis nominibus appellanda sunt, haud aliter quàm panis panis, vinum vinũ, corpus corpus, sanguis sanguis, dicenda sunt. Comparatè spectata, ad eum rerum ordinem pertinent quæ aliò referûtur: unde cùm mutuã affectionem quandam acquirant, debebant utique noua etiam nomina sortiri, acquisitam affectionem indicātia: quemadmodum duo homines, quo ad substantiam, homines sunt atque dicuntur: accedente vero noua conditione aliqua, unus dicitur dominus, alter seruus: unus præceptor, alter discipulus, &c. Ad eundem modum panis & vinum in cœna Domini, assumpta & segregata in sigilla corporis & sanguinis Domini, etsi priora nomina unà cum pristina substantia sua retinent: ex institutione tamen Domini hoc assequuntur ut panis & vinum Domini vocentur. Sic Augustinus scribit, Judam proditorem potuit se mäducare panem Domini, at non panem Dominum. Panis Domini, est τὸ σῶμα τῆς π[?]: panis Dominus, est τὸ ἀντί-σρέφον[?]. Fundamentum igitur, est panis & vini substantia: terminus, est corpus & sanguis Christi: relatio inter hæc, est fundamenti ad terminum applicatio & analogia. quæ sic exponi potest: Quod in hac vita temporaria corpori humano fame sitíque propemodum ene&to[?] panis & vinum seu cibus & potus sunt, hoc interiori homini sensu propriae iniustitiae tantum non exhausto ac desperabundo corpus & san-guis Christi sunt.
units.tr: These two kinds of things set forth in the Lord's Supper may be considered in two ways: absolutely and comparatively. Considered absolutely, the visible elements, bread and wine, and the invisible grace, that is, the body and blood of Christ, belong to the category of substances. In this respect they keep their natural names, as they were first given, and claim them as their own. So if bread and wine, and likewise the body and blood of Christ, are to be called by their proper names, they must be called bread bread, wine wine, body body, and blood blood. Considered comparatively, they belong to that order of things which refer to something else. Since they therefore acquire a certain borrowed relation, they ought also to receive new names indicating the acquired relation. So two men, as to substance, are and are called men; but when some new condition is added, one is called master and the other servant, one teacher and the other disciple, and so on. In the same way, bread and wine in the Lord's Supper, taken up and set apart as signs of the body and blood of the Lord, keep their former names along with their former substance; yet by the institution of the Lord they obtain this, that they are called the bread and wine of the Lord. So Augustine writes that Judas the traitor could eat the bread of the Lord, but not the Lord's bread [Panis Domini est τὸ σῶμα τῆς π…; panis Dominus est τὸ ἀντίτυπον]. The foundation, then, is the substance of bread and wine; the term is the body and blood of Christ; the relation between these is the application and analogy of the foundation to the term. This may be explained thus: as in this temporal life bread and wine, or food and drink, are what nourish the human body, which is almost worn out by hunger and thirst, so the body and blood of Christ are what the inner man, exhausted and despairing through the sense of his own unrighteousness, is nourished by.

units.la: Peccatum & iniustitia æternâ mortem homini afferunt, nisi Christus suo corpore pro nobis tradito & sanguine in remissionem peccatorum nostrorum profuso, peccata nostra obliteret, nobisque esurientibus sitientibusque iustitiam, sua satisfactione & obedientia patri pro nobis præstita in ignominiosissimam mortem crucis vsq;, defectum suppleat. Huius igitur per fidem facti participes, refocillamur, & vitam denique æternam cosequimur.
units.tr: Sin and unrighteousness bring eternal death upon man, unless Christ, with his body given up for us and his blood poured out for the forgiveness of our sins, blots out our sins and, to us who hunger and thirst for righteousness, supplies what is lacking, by his satisfaction and his obedience rendered to the Father on our behalf, even to the most shameful death of the cross. Those who by faith are made partakers of this are refreshed, and at last they obtain eternal life.

units.la: DOMINVS noster Iesus Christus interpellans pro discipulis & to to credentium grege patrem, inter alia sic orat, Sanctifica eos in veritate tua: sermo tuus veritas est. Cùm igitur Ecclesiastes Salomonis, vna sententia, & recte quidem, omnes omnium opiniones, fœlicitate hominis extra Deum quærentes aut ponentes, vanitatis damnet, & vt falsas & perniciosas reprobet: merito etiam præfertur Dei verbum reliquis doctrinis & scriptis omnibus, vel hoc solo nomine, quòd nusquam alibi quàm in scriptura sacra, sapientia diuinæ atque æternæ veritatis inueniatur. Vnde & Apostolus in Ecclesia nihil aliud nisi vocem æterni Dei sonare vult, quando sic præcipit, Si quis loquitur, vt eloquia Dei loquatur. Quoties ergo de veritate & sapientia infallibili quæstio incidit, curram⁹ ad fontem illum viuū scripturarum, ac inde hauriamus quantum opus fit & sufficiat siti nostræ leuandæ ac re-stinguendæ.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ, interceding with the Father for his disciples and the whole flock of believers, prays among other things: "Sanctify them in your truth; your word is truth." Since the Ecclesiastes of Solomon, in one saying, and rightly, condemns as vanity all the opinions of men that seek or place human happiness outside God, and rejects them as false and pernicious, so the Word of God is rightly preferred to all other doctrines and all other writings, if only for this reason, that the wisdom of divine and eternal truth is found nowhere else than in Holy Scripture. Hence the Apostle also wishes that nothing but the voice of the eternal God should sound in the Church, when he commands: "If anyone speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God." Whenever, therefore, a question of truth and infallible wisdom arises, let us run to that living fountain of the Scriptures, and draw from it as much as is needed and sufficient to allay and quench our thirst.

units.la: Gloriabantur quidem Judæi lege & verbo Dei, scriptis(inquā) Mosis & Prophetarum, in quibus videbantur sibi vitam æternam habere, profite-bantúrque se Dei voluntatem scire: quia verò factis negabant, abomina-biles Deo facti sunt. Verbū ergo Dei æstimandum est magis virtute, quàm sono: quippe multis dicentibus Chri-sto, Domine, Domine: responsurus est Christus in illo die, Non novi vos: cùm tamen testetur Apostolus neminem posse dicere dominum esse Jesum, ni-si per Spiritum sanctum. Sed hæc con-sessio si verbo tenus fieri intelligenda est, tunc non nudus verbi sonus, sed & sensus & virtus coniunctim cum ver-bo accipitur. Stulta verò est iactantia literæ mortuæ & à spiritu & genuino sensu separatæ: quemadmodum Ju-dæi scripturam sibi viuificam esse pu-tabant, tabant, sed absque uiuificante spiritu & iusta eius intelligentia, cùm in hūc finem & usum scriptura diuinitus de-stinata esset, ut vita æterna in illa quę [?]reretur. Quoniam autem non ubique in superficie scripturæ mens scriptu-ræ inuenitur, opus est scrutinio, ut ne quod in profundo latet, nobis rema-neat absconditum. Si quis ergo verbū Dei neglectim audiēs aut scripturam obiter quasi in transcursu & superfi-cie inspiciens, mox sanctam illam veritatem se tenere & percepisse arbi-tretur, is fallit seipsum, lucē uitæ quæ illic continetur sibi obscurans & præ-focans. Nec putandus est talis debitū honorem deferre Dei verbo, qui hæ-rens in cortice literæ seu nuda voce, ad medullam & nucleum eius intel-lectu nō penetrat. Et rursus, non mox à verbo Dei & scriptura recedere cen-sendus est, qui omisso literæ cortice, thesaurum diuinæ mentis ibi recon-ditum inquirit aut ostendit.
units.tr: The Jews indeed boasted in the law and the word of God, namely the writings of Moses and the Prophets, in which they seemed to have eternal life, and they professed that they knew the will of God; but because they denied it by their deeds, they became abominable to God. The word of God is therefore to be valued for its power rather than its sound: for when many say to Christ, "Lord, Lord," Christ will answer on that day, "I never knew you"; yet the Apostle testifies that no one can say that Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit. But if this confession is to be understood as merely verbal, then it is not the bare sound of the word but its sense and power that are taken together with the word. Foolish indeed is the boasting of the dead letter, separated from the Spirit and its genuine sense; just as the Jews thought Scripture was life-giving to them, but without the life-giving Spirit and its right understanding, although Scripture was divinely appointed for this end and use, that eternal life should be sought in it. Since, moreover, the mind of Scripture is not everywhere found on the surface of Scripture, there is need of searching, lest what lies hidden in the depths remain concealed from us. If anyone hears the Word of God carelessly, or looks at Scripture only in passing, as it were in transit and on the surface, and straightway thinks he holds and has perceived that holy truth, he deceives himself, darkening and choking the light of life that is contained there. Nor is he to be thought to pay the due honour to the Word of God who clings to the bark of the letter or the bare voice and does not penetrate by understanding to its marrow and kernel. And again, he is not to be judged as departing from the Word of God and Scripture who, setting aside the bark of the letter, seeks out or shows the treasure of the divine mind hidden there.
